Current state-of-the-art language models represent common words through specific vectors, but less common words often get lumped together with irrelevant meanings due to their inherent rarity. As a result, advanced models struggle to effectively represent rare words, but research shows this can be improved by incorporating context, specifically from parallel corpora composed of aggregated datasets that include both source and multiple target languages. Given that parallel corpora often contain a mixture of target languages and noise, the self-supervised learning approach can help filter out irrelevant information and improve rare word representations. Our proposed method, JEN - Learning to Identify and Represent Novel Equations from parallel Corpora, utilizes a neural model that leverages aligned data to identify and refine the context-based representations of rare words across multiple target languages. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique enhances context-based representations of rare words, ultimately leading to substantial gains in translating data-rich languages to data-poor languages, and yields substantial improvements in translating data-rich languages to data-poor languages, specifically by 4.6-14.2 EM and 3.1-13.2 BLEU. Moreover, our analysis reveals that our method successfully decomposes noise by 25-31% and boosts the understanding of rare words by 43-163%. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ziyi2018/JEN. Furthermore, our analysis shows that our method successfully extracts contextual information and improves the understanding of novel equations, specifically by 25-31% in terms of noise reduction and 43-163% in terms of rare word representations. As an added benefit, our method can also be applied to other neural machine translation benefits, such as transferring knowledge to highly resource-scarce languages like Japanese and Neapolitan. Interestingly, our experiments show our method achieves notable performance gains in translating data-rich languages to data-poor languages, specifically by 3.1-13.2 BLEU. Interestingly, our study discovered that our technique could successfully transfer knowledge from high resource-scarce languages, specifically Japanese and Neapolitan, to other target languages, and yielded significant performance improvements, with BLEU gains of 3.1, 10.9, and 2.5 when translating English to Japanese, Neapolitan, and German respectively. These gains were often accompanied by consistent and substantial improvements in English-Japanese and German translations. Notably, our method showed promising performance in translating data-poor languages to other target languages, specifically by 10.9, 14.2, and 3.5 BLE

Research on graph structures known as Minimum Spanning Acycles has been explored, particularly through a weighted model involving random edge costs. Similar to the case with Euclidean Minimum Spanning Acycles, researchers have demonstrated the existence of distinct extreme weight categories within this model. This study focuses on investigating the statistical convergence of these extreme weight categories and develops a corresponding model of a weighted cycle in which researchers can prove convergence of a key statistical model. Additionally, researchers have obtained new insights into cycles of the shortest length in random graphs and extended existing findings related to Euclidean Minimum Spanning Acycles, thereby shedding light on a long-standing open problem in this area. Further investigation of this model has also enabled researchers to develop a new method for verifying a key statistical model of extreme weight categories, known as the Flory formula. This study establishes a relationship between this model and a novel Gibbs distribution, thereby proving the convergence of this model to the Gibbs distribution. Researchers have further validated the convergence of this model to the Euclidean Minimum Spanning Acycle by proving its statistical equivalence to a Euclidean Minimum Spanning Acycle under specific conditions. This study has also delved into exploring its model's applicability to other graph structures and found that it can be effectively used in two distinct scenarios: to develop a new model of extreme weight categories for a specific type of graph known as the Hamming lattice; to develop a new model of extreme weight categories for a specific type of graph known as the bipartite random maximum acyclic matching. This study further delves into exploring its model's applicability to other graph structures and finds that these are just two out of numerous other distinct graph structures that can be effectively explored using this approach. 

A substantially extended version of this study can be found at arXiv:2206.11698, in which researchers have obtained new insights into Bipartite Minimum Spanning Acycles and developed a new model of extreme weight categories for a specific type of graph known as the bipartite Minimum Spanning Acycles. This study further delves into exploring its model's applicability to other graph structures and finds that Bipartite Minimum Spanning Acycles represent a particularly suitable test case for assessing the efficacy and consistency of the developed approach.

This research showcases the feasibility of privacy attacks on a custom federated learning protocol tailored for internet-of-things devices, especially when implementing vertical federated learning protocols. We developed a simple yet effective attack that could pinpoint the specific institution owning each data record in most cases. Additionally, our attack could predict the specific institution providing a training dataset with high accuracy for both continuous and discrete data types. We applied the attack using real-world data sets from the MIMIC-U2F and MIMIC-III databases. These attacks were carried out using agglomerative clustering, simple threshold methods, and graph-based approaches. We considered the computational constraints of internet-of-things devices when implementing the attack methods. A UT-2 microcontroller was used to evaluate the processing time and resources utilization, which showed the attack can be executed in under 60 milliseconds while consuming around 55% of the device's capabilities. This demonstrates the vulnerability of vertical federated learning to privacy attacks surpassing previous research, at the same time highlighting the efficiency of the attack from a resource standpoint for internet-of-things devices. We create a video showing how the attack works and upload it to https://youtu.be/ODtT1S3TLGk, also providing code and data at https://github/UofT-GAFA/tree/UT-GAFA-MIMIC. We propose a simple method to mitigate this type of attack that can be easily implemented by researchers using vertical federated learning. This method involves providing a fake dataset when participating in vertical federated learning, which was tested and shown to effectively prevent the attack as well as not impacting the model's performance when applied to a regression task using the MIMIC-U2F data sets. We highlight a notable limitation of vertical federated learning which might have a considerable impact on its feasibility for the internet-of-things domain. This research aims to raise awareness about the feasibility of privacy attacks on vertical federated learning and discusses potential strategies to mitigate these attacks, highlighting achievable improvements in this field.

Urban areas are increasingly vulnerable to terrorist attacks of a magnitude capable of wreaking havoc on major events, essential infrastructure and entire neighborhoods. As regional authorities struggle to counter an escalating terrorist threat, what resources should they allocate to maximize their defenses? In this study, a budget allocation model was devised to optimize the security provided by a urban area's comprehensive terrorism-defence system. Leveraging a finite-state Markov process combined with a reinforcement learning algorithm based on Q-learning, the model allows key urban authorities to direct limited resources with maximum efficacy by identifying optimal state transitions and reward structures. Simulation results demonstrate that by allocating their resources according to this optimal policy, a significant 15.13% increase in the overall quality of city-wide security can be achieved. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that different agencies may require varying levels of cross cooperation, and that prioritizing information sharing among them is crucial to achieving optimal defences. Finally, by integrating this optimal policy into a parallel parallel distributed processing model, the distribution of resources required to achieve this optimal policy among city agencies was identified. The proposed model is validated through Monte Carlo simulations. Results show that by allocating their resources according to this optimal policy, a significant 15.13% increase in the overall quality of city-wide security can be achieved. The paper concludes that the proposed model is versatile and can be easily adapted to various real-world applications by utilizing simulated scenarios and incorporating expert knowledge to represent complex interactions between regional authorities and their environment. Examples of applicable domains are presented throughout the paper. Firstly, the model will be applied to investigate resource allocation with a view to optimising urban rainfall collection and retention. Secondly, the model will be used to explore the automation of Windows 10 operating-system updates in order to gain valuable insights into how the frequency of updates impacts system stability and the potential impact on user activity. Finally, the model will be used to gain a deeper understanding of the complexities of multi-agent negotiation by applying it to a real-world automated multi-agent negotiation scenario. These diverse examples serve to solidify the model's broad generalizability. Furthermore, the model's efficacy was enhanced through the incorporation of a dynamic programming-based correction mechanism, which helps to minimize its reliance on simulation results. Lastly, the study outlines avenues for future research, where the model's relevance to unattended surveillance systems in urban environments is discussed, paving the way for potential future studies to reveal more insights into the inherent trade-offs involved in optimizing resource allocation for these systems. This paper introduces a new sampling method called bag sampling that reduces the requirement for large collections of redundant documents in search engine indexting, thus facilitating better ranking for lengthy documents. By using a cutting-plane method, we demonstrate that bag sampling can effectively minimize the number of duplicate documents, thereby increasing the long document ranking precision. Experimental results obtained from TREC datasets show that ranking performance for both long and general queries can benefit from the proposed bag sampling approach. Notably, we observed a significant improvement in long document ranking precision for the benchmarks pubmed2016 and voicereport, with gains of 9.0% and 11.1% respectively over the current state-of-the-art model. Moreover, bag sampling outperformed a cutting-edge compression technique recently proposed compression-aided ranking (CAR), achieving a 1.0% higher precision on the benchmark pubmed2016. The proposed bag sampling method has been incorporated into the FuseRank ranking system, enabling it to successfully participate in the TREC 2020 long document ranking campaign. All source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/dancingnube/FuseRank/tree/fags2022. Additionally, we released an open-source tool for the bag sampling method, which can be accessed at https://github.com/dancingnube/BagSampling. This tool allows users to optimize an index with a pre-existing ranking function, while minimizing the required document collection, thus yielding better ranking performance. The proposed bag sampling method has been optimized to work effectively with the top-ranking ranking methods, demonstrating great potential in enhancing search engine performance through the retrieval of large collections of documents. Furthermore, we theorize that bag sampling can be universally beneficial for all ranking functions, including those yet unknown. In the knowledge graph setting, we observed that bag sampling can efficiently minimize the requirement for numerous redundant entities in the index, thereby paving the way for substantial reductions in indexing cost. Notably, this has been proven theoretically in the context of entity-based search, where it is shown that a distinct bag sampling approach can be used to recover an exact ranking function from a subset of entities. The proposed theory therefore contributes to the understanding of ranking function compression as an inverse problem, enabling a search algorithm to identify the essential components required from a large collection of data. The simplicity and efficacy of the proposed bag sampling method have enabled it to outperform other recent compression techniques in entity-based search, with significant gains in precision. Experimental results obtained from TREC datasets show that bag sampling can effectively minimize the requirement for redundant entities

We analyzed pseudo-labeling's influence on semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks and found that currently used methods are inadequate. We developed an alternative method known as NodeSmart, which utilizes community membership to create high-quality pseudo labels by eliminating labeling inconsistencies. NodeSmart enhances the robustness of GNNs in face of incorrect labels by minimizing labeling discrepancies. We tested NodeSmart across various scenarios and found it outperforms existing methods significantly, showcasing its effectiveness. The source code for NodeSmart is available at https://github.com/Researchers39/NodeSmart. Our project aims to expand NodeSmart applications to address semi-supervised node regression challenges in the future. Additionally, we suggest pseudo-labeling's impact on GNNs should be reevaluated in other tasks such as link prediction and unsupervised graph representation learning. The semi-supervised learning process can be optimized by leveraging pseudo-labeling effectively, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy to help researchers develop more effective methods, thereby enhancing GNN robustness and accuracy. The interaction between betatron radiation and plasma wakefield acceleration is analyzed, revealing how electron beam performance influences the focused beam trajectory and radiation pattern. A critical factor, radial mismatch between the electron beam and plasma wake, is found to impact beam dynamics significantly. Research demonstrates that by adjusting the electron beam's charge and initial radial offset, an optimal focused beam can be achieved, yielding an enhanced emittance. Furthermore, it has been confirmed that reduced phase modulation of the focused beam can improve betatron radiation intensity and, consequently, particle detection capabilities. As a means of experimental validation, an implementation of a two-stage plasma cell setup has been proposed, which can be utilized to study and optimize this particle acceleration technique. A comprehensive review of the beam dynamics and radiation patterns for various electron beam settings in this plasma cell setup is provided through simulation results. The potential also exists for this plasma cell setup to serve as a highly sensitive radiation intensity detector. The study's findings are set against the background of an ongoing experiment, MIRA-Hello-World, where researchers are engaged in plasma wakefield acceleration studies. A supplementary document containing further information on the MIRA-Hello-World experiment and simulation data can be accessed at www.mira-hi.de/HellowWorld. We investigate the convergence behavior of uniformly convergent hypotheses in relation to differentially private decision tree learning. Our results reveal that this convergence is achievable and, in a critical finding, highly accurate decision trees can be learned from significantly large datasets, albeit with lower accuracy than in the non-private case, due to increased noise when smaller deviations occur. Our results are based on a novel, refined convergence inequality that improves upon a previously established result by Castro et al. from 2016. Our study also extends to cover sequentially generated hypothesis classes, allowing for better analysis of decision trees that adapt to data streams. Utilizing a recent improvement by Gupta et al. from 2019, we found that our new inequality is comparable in the context of adaptive hypothesis classes. Our research also demonstrates the applicability of our new inequality to privacy in the Euclidean space, given that Castro et al.'s inequality is subsumed by earlier results from Dwork et al. from 2010. Our study introduces a crucial distinction between hypothesis classes with bounded or unbounded deviations, revealing that differentially private learning for classes with unbounded deviations may never produce a hypothesis with zero error. Our results are demonstrated through application to an initially introduced synthetic dataset and an examination of the primary factors influencing private learning accuracy. Our findings show that both dataset size and the prior confidence in a hypothesis play a role in accurate private learning. Our study concludes with a strategy to leverage private learning to create more accurate hypotheses when prior knowledge is limited, thereby reducing error and increasing the effectiveness of hypotheses. Our results are realized through an open-source library. Our research offers an established bound on the deviation of differentially private learning and sets a baseline for further research into non-asymptotic analysis of uniformly convergent hypothesis classes, an area previously lacking such important non-asymptotic results in the field of differential privacy. This paper introduces a novel model selection method called product Dirichlet priors for assessing the number of conditional probability tables in a chain event graph. We demonstrate that this approach yields an objective Bayesian belief function equivalent to the normalised maximum marginal likelihood, providing a useful alternative to existing model selection techniques for chain event graphs. Like other methods, product Dirichlet priors facilitate spatially mixture-based model selection where the optimal model can lie outside the specified prior distribution. Compared to other methods, product Dirichlet priors demonstrate a clearer objective function and more effective model selection in various synthetic and real-world datasets, including amyloid beta protein and Dutch polder flooding. The product Dirichlet priors' computational efficiency makes them suitable for large datasets. The method is made available through an R package called peg.IDL. The package also includes the junction tree algorithm and other useful tools for chain event graph modelling and selection. The source code for the product Dirichlet method is open-source and can be accessed at github.com/tmcmthy/MCMCPEG/tree/product-dirichlet. The method is also available for use in mgp package for Gaussian process regression, allowing a marginalization of the junction tree model over the Gaussian process parameters. The product Dirichlet priors' computational time is largely determined by the data-driven computation of the marginal junction tree belief tree, with a complexity of O(N^2.5K) for a dataset of size N and K conditional probability tables. The method's efficiency is further improved by sampling from the junction tree distribution, with an empirical variance of 1/(K+1), indicating a reliable point estimation can be achieved with a small sample size. The method is shown to be nearly independent of model hyperparameters such as the dataset's clusterability and the latent cluster sizes. The method's empirical power for false discovery is shown to be robust to varying prior concentrations, with a p-value approximation accurate to the first three decimal places. The method shows a surprising discovery rate of 83% for amyloid beta protein and Dutch polder flooding, with an estimated p-value of 2.2e-16 and 1.3e-14 respectively, indicating a very strong evidence against the null hypothesis of no spatial effect. cuprate superconductors in the normal and superconducting states.  A unique
microscopic model for undoped cuprates and the optimal doping levels in superconducting cuprates have been introduced, with the key feature being a finite self-consistent chemical potential.  Calculations show that the usual approximation for conductivity in the normal state breaks down near the electron to cuprate hole transition.  In the superconducting state, the assumption that the superconducting energy gap is relatively small compared to the cuprate bandwidth also fails.  Both computational methods yield similar results: in both cases, a finite self-consistent chemical potential significantly alters the physics.  The effect of the superconducting gap on conductivity at low temperatures is reduced compared to the optimal doping levels, whereas it is enhanced at higher temperatures. We explore the stability of the emergence model by examining the behavior of nonlinear perturbations. Our analysis reveals that the model's stability is akin to a different theoretical framework, the quartic Thaw model, although the onset of ghost instability in the emergence model is delayed. Furthermore, a mode coupling analysis adds support to our initial findings. We also investigate the potential consequences of ghost instability on the nonlinear sector of the emergence model and propose a possible real-world analogy in the behavior of an unstable sound wave on the surface of deep water. Ultimately, a thorough assessment of the model's stability requirements in relation to its cosmological applicability is warranted. Our research aims to contribute to this assessment, but a thorough validation of the model would necessitate additional tools, such as a linear perturbation analysis. Such an investigation is also crucial to determining whether the emergence model can satisfy all the conditions necessary for a successful cosmic reconstruction as a candidate theory of dark energy.

Pontryagin's principle offers a powerful method for creating and testing hypotheses related to Nash equilibrium in complex systems like vehicle platoons. By utilizing this principle, researchers can identify key factors that influence equilibrium points, like maximum following distance. An existing study demonstrated the principle's effectiveness in analyzing Nash equilibrium through the use of optimal control techniques. Building upon this foundation, we develop a set of necessary conditions for equilibrium points, leveraging the principles of subdifferentiation and variational calculus. Our analysis reveals that these conditions can be interpreted as the linear time-invariant system governing vehicle following in platoons, further highlighting the principle's utility in this context. Ultimately, we discuss potential future applications of this formal approach, including examining the impact of homogeneity on Nash equilibrium and its implications for automated vehicle systems. An oral presentation of this research, including additional details, is available online through the arXiv platform at https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10387. The corresponding code for this work can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/CAT-SI.ARJ/nash-equilibrium-optimality-conditions. Additionally, a publicly accessible Docker container provides supporting simulations to validate the findings. As the field of vehicle automation rapidly advances, improving the robustness and reliability of decision-making systems is crucial, necessitating a deeper understanding of the underlying principles and mathematical frameworks. By integrating set-theoretic approaches to subdifferentiation and Pontryagin's principle, we strive to develop highly transparent, interpretable, and explainable automation systems for vehicle application. Nevertheless, our analysis currently appears to be the first manifestation of Nash equilibrium in a specific system according to Pontryagin's principle. This research evaluates whether a unique approach can pinpoint authored content, specifically comparing human-written and computer-generated headlines and articles. A dataset was compiled with 1,036 articles and 1,531,908 sentences and phrases that vary in authorship, including 606,602 produced by crowdsourced humans and 301,406 generated by AI. A BERT-based model was trained to discern between these three categories, yielding accurate assessments in three domains - natural language, text style, and content type. Furthermore, analysis revealed that the model was most adept at distinguishing computer-generated content, suggesting that its distinctive style poses the greatest threat in authorship manipulation. In contrast, instances of human-generated text that deceive as being written by another human are relatively few and distinct in style. Interestingly, the study found that the AI-generated text often shares similarities with news headlines, indicating that the threat may be more pronounced in this specific context, although this needs to be further investigated. Overall, the research shows that current AI models are effective in identifying authored content, but the inverse - distinguishing generated from human-authored content - remains an unresolved challenge. This could pose serious implications, such as allowing users to block AI-generated content, prevent widespread dissemination of misinformation, and evade targeted attacks via computer-generated text attacks, given their evident ability to evade current detection by existing models. In light of this, the research recommends exploring more sophisticated transformer-based architectures that incorporate contextual and semantic knowledge to enhance the capability to pinpoint authored content, especially in preventing misuse of computer-generated text attacks. A novel open-source computer-generated text attack model was also proposed, enabling the simulation of attacks that evade detection by current models and demonstrate existing vulnerabilities. Consequently, the research outlines avenues for future research to boost the capability to discern between generated and authored content, specifically suggesting the use of the developed dataset, the application of more sophisticated transformer-based architectures, and the integration of contextual and semantic knowledge. Furthermore, the research proposes a new open-source computer-generated text attack model, allowing for simulation of attacks that are resistant to detection by current models and highlight existing vulnerabilities, thereby paving the way for future research directions. In conclusion, while the results show the effectiveness of transformer models in distinguishing generated and human-authored content, the inverse challenge remains an unresolved challenge, posing significant theoretical and practical threats, suggesting the necessity for further research directions. We have developed a series of research papers building on earlier foundations, whereas a different approach is presented here, inspired by a previously established community detection method in hypergraphs. Our solution starts with a data structure known as hyperlet, which is derived from the tensor join of a hypergraph and its subgraphs of varying rank. We utilize this data structure to design a community detection method that leverages a hypergraph's two-level relaxation process. By applying our data structure, we are able to calculate relaxation parameters directly from the hypergraph's boundary tensor, thereby improving detection efficiency. We utilize the node potentials and tensor values stored in the data structure for parameter recovery in cases where the relaxation parameters are unknown. Finally, our work serves as an alternative to existing hypergraph algorithms, providing a more efficient solution. The results show, for instance, that the average speed of a Riesz process, which is a stochastic process described by a diffusion equation with coefficient |x|^{d-1}, can be bounded by a polynomial function of the diffusion dimension d and the time t, as long as d is greater than or equal to 1. To effectively navigate crowded spaces, robots necessitate a sophisticated collision avoidance system, especially in environments where navigating safely is equivalent to navigating quickly. Present collision avoidance methods usually rely on a straightforward estimation of the likelihood of collisions, resulting in a conservative approach that prioritizes safety over efficiency. We propose an enhanced strategy that considers not only the probability of collisions but also the precision of the probability estimates in the prediction model to determine safe navigation paths. We demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing methods utilizing a single or dual dynamic models in both simulation and real-life testing on a mobile robot. The accompanying video visualizes the different collision avoidance techniques employed by the robot. The source code is publicly accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/krati/peccar.

The luminous red giant branch segment of the Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Andromeda XXV, has been analyzed to study its brightness and metal content. Based on 2018 observations with the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3 instrument, Andromeda XXV's magnitude and color data have been obtained for 15 red giant stars. These observations enable an accurate measurement of the galaxy's total luminosity, surface brightness, and mass-to-light ratio. Notably, Andromeda XXV's mass-to-light ratio is significantly higher than typical dwarf spheroidal galaxies, suggesting a more pronounced luminosity difference between first and second bright red giant stars. This discrepancy is likely attributed to a relatively high velocity dispersion of Andromeda XXV. Further analysis of the galaxy's velocity dispersion and random velocity reveals a relatively high value of 14.5 km/s, one of the highest in its class. Using isochrones that have been shifted in color to match the galaxy's metallicity, the galaxy's age has been determined to be around 13 billion years old. These properties make Andromeda XXV unique among low-luminosity dwarf galaxies with similar metal content. Moreover, the galaxy's luminosity and brightness exhibit a strong negative correlation when compared to similar galaxies, further establishing its distinct characteristics. These findings contribute to our understanding of the galaxy's formation and evolution, placing Andromeda XXV among the older population of dwarf galaxies in the Local Group. A comparison of Andromeda XXV's brightness and mass over a long period would provide significant insights into the galaxy's depletion rate of gas over its lifetime. Lastly, the galaxy's velocity dispersion, mass-to-light ratio, and age have been added to the Dwarf Galaxies, Galaxy Groups, and clusters database. These findings reveal that the galaxy's metal content is relatively low, around one-hundredth of the sun's metal content. This measurement makes Andromeda XXV one of the most metal-poor dwarf galaxies in its class with similar brightness. We introduce the concept of $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebras as an extension of traditional exterior and symmetric algebras through the utilization of the $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$ system of Khashimoto. This class of algebras is then explored in the context of general matrices, resulting in the observation that exterior coefficients replicate the principle of inclusion-exclusion while symmetric coefficients adhere to the principle of inclusion-exclusion twice. Additionally, these $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebras are established as a matroidal framework by Lopez's criteria. Lastly, the determinantal structure within these $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebras is shown to be intact when reduced to the realm of finite fields, much like Kapranov's field. This framework offers an alternative understanding of finite fields, characterized by non-negative determinants. Yet, in contrast, the realm of real numbers is represented by a specific $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$-algebra where determinants exhibit a negative aspect as well. Building on the comparison between real and finite fields, the notion of a log-scheme is explored through the interpretation of the $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$ system as a one-dimensional one. We propose replacing traditional coordinate systems with an underlying combinatorial structure, suggesting Schur positiveness could serve as an ideal criterion for navigation within the realm of real numbers, while determinantal negativity might facilitate navigation within finite fields, and the underlying underlying logic of $\mathbb{Z}$ can be generalized through the $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$ system. Lastly, the issue of real numbers containing the roots 'one' and '-one' remains an unsolved problem in the realm of real numbers. Our work proposes resolving this problem by introducing a specific case where real roots do exist, much like the roots found within positive definite matrices, through the process of taking an exterior symmetric square. This proposed case can be generalized and applied universally by exploring the situation where all coefficients across the entire domain are positive, an instance that can be realized within positive definite matrices, then taking an exterior square, and finally factorizing along a specific Schur-positive pattern. Recent dialogue state tracking models rely heavily on data-generated labels for training. Although supervised learning methods produce satisfactory results, they're limited by the availability of high-quality labels. Self-supervised learning offers a solution by freeing models from reliance on data labels. Our approach generates unfitted data with masked labels that preserve the temporal relationship of dialogue states. This is achieved through two transforms. First, we introduce an attentional confusion network to encode dialogue records with a higher level of abstraction, enhancing dialogue state fitting. Second, we generate masked labels that mimic those of fit datasets, allowing our model to be trained with a separate module for each state component. Our proposed method outperforms existing self-supervised Dialogue State Tracking baselines on the DSTC 2 and 3 datasets. Additionally, we observe that combining unfitted data with labeled data leads to improved performance in fit-learning settings. This study demonstrates that self-supervised learning can effectively produce informative data for training Dialogue State Tracking models. On the other hand, the combination of this approach with fit-training data enhances model performance, leading to a competitive outcome with a fit-trained baseline model. The regularised sum of points, weighted by Hodge polynomials of Hilbert schemes, can be utilized to calculate more precise invariants related to the moduli space of stable vector bundles, specifically those with rank r and Chern classes as well as a Kähler class. This has led to the discovery of novel gauge theoretical invariants. Furthermore, it is found that these regularised sums cancel out flux contributions in the dual BPS limit, in contrast to standard point counts which yield an overestimate due to wall-crossing effects. Moreover, the regularised sum formula extends to the more general case of moduli of sheaf representations, and its derivation involves reduction to surjective morphisms from projective spaces. Additionally, it is shown that for any given n, the regularised sum of points on P^n can be expressed in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials and their analogues, with coefficients related to the Gromov-Witten Thom-Seiberg residues. This new finding introduces the concept of regularised primary and derived invariants, and their correlation with usual measures. It is observed that the derived regularised sum of points exhibits asymmetry, as manifested through its expression involving alternating elementary symmetric polynomials, hinting at distinct behaviour for even and odd values of n. The study also explores its connection to the moduli of rank 1 sheaves and identifies a connection to the Weil-Petersson metric via a singular curvature representation, as discovered by Haraldsson-Zhang. Moreover, it is discovered that at the BPS limit, the asymptotic behaviour of the regularised sum formula relates to the BPS state orthogonality graph and yields an exact value, as opposed to standard point counts which yield an overestimate due to wall-crossing effects. Consistency of the derived regularised approach has been verified by comparing it to the known facts about regularised sums for curve counting problems and shows that it generalises to the more complex case of discovering wall-crossing invariant of vector-bundle moduli, an area where such generalisation was hitherto unknown before this study. It is also hypothesised that such generalisation should also extend to the more complex case of discovering wall-crossing invariant of sheaf-representation moduli, an area that is yet to be explored before this study. The conclusion drawn from such generalisation indicates that such approach is likely to be an efficient method for finding new and novel mathematical theorems and results, as well as providing a deeper understanding of existing ones. Our research focuses on the structural characteristics of secret-sharing schemes known as access structures. The complexity of an access structure, specifically for schemes with a fixed number of minimal qualified groups, was previously studied byishikawa, Matsumoto, Matsumoto, and Yamada - they showed that for a certain type of access structure, the complexity decreased exponentially with the number of minimal groups when the order of the groups was two. We build upon their work by considering a broader class of access structures and provide a more general estimate of the complexity by comparing it to a known lower limit, thus proving that the previous findings were not the only possible outcomes. Furthermore, our results show that the complexity of a particular type of access structure can either decrease exponentially with the number of minimal groups or increase logarithmically when the order of the groups is greater than two. We also investigate the complexity for a different type of access structure with varying numbers of minimal groups and find the possible behaviors of the complexity decreasing exponentially with the number of minimal groups or increasing arithmetically. 
We also study universal access structures with a fixed number of minimal qualified groups and derive an asymptotic estimate of the complexity by comparing it to a known lower limit, thus proving that the previous findings of Matsumoto, et al. were a specific instance of this general result.

In this research, we investigate the effectiveness of Nearest Mean Classifier, which achieves high performance with limited memory, matching state-of-the-art results in most cases, yet in some situations, it slightly lags behind. Notably, NM-CRE is an in-depth continuation of our previous contribution to Incremental Learning, where we found that increasing the out-of-distribution detection overlap results in improved task boundaries identification. Consequently, we have optimized the Nearest Mean Classifier to produce cleaner task boundaries by incorporating an enhanced overlap metric, thereby reducing boundary ambiguity and increasing performance in relevant scenarios. Our proposed modifications to NM-CRE, specifically incorporating an optimized metric, yield improved performance and cleaner transitions, yet we observe a natural compromise between task boundaries clarity and retained old knowledge when employing this classifier. Importantly, our contribution sheds light on the simplicity and efficiency of NM-CRE as well as its seamless integration and fast training capabilities, making it very attractive for real-world applications involving the memories of deep neural networks. Language models bear the hallmarks of the society that created them, a fact
that is particularly evident in the content they generate. This phenomenon is
known as the socio-cultural imprint. While typically considered an issue
involving language model biases, socio-cultural imprinting has far-reaching
consequences. This study explores the socio-cultural imprint of languages
as hate speech detection systems. We demonstrate that models trained to
detect hate speech in one language are also likely to do so in other languages
due to shared socio-cultural connections. However, this can lead to
unintended consequences such as labelling harmless content as hateful. We
perform an extensive investigation across 11 languages and 15 hate speech
categories using 192 language models and highlight the need for more
sophisticated socio-cultural awareness in hate speech detection systems to
mitigate harmful impacts in diverse cultural contexts. The research dataset
can be found at https://github.com/mixed-ai/hate-speech-socio-imprint. This
research aims to contribute to a better comprehension of language models as
social products that necessitate careful consideration of their socio-cultural
imprint in hate speech detection applications. Furthermore, our results
illustrate the complexity of deploying hate speech detection systems that are
sensitive to socio-cultural differences without adequate tools for accurate
socio-cultural awareness assessment and mitigation. To address these gaps,
we suggest developing and leveraging domain-specific dictionaries and
distributed word representations that account for socio-cultural imprint. While
these solutions can help mitigate biases, they do come with limitations such
as dictionary errors and representation limitations. Therefore, we suggest
that the development of more sophisticated socio-cultural awareness modules
remains an important goal despite existing limitations. We estimate that
reducing the error rate of such modules could result in substantial
improvements of hate speech detection accuracy, a consideration that should
be explored in future research. The research also highlights the need for
accountability in the deployment of automated hate speech detection tools,

Collective oscillations in network electrophysiology, such as synchronized heart rhythms and collective cardiac arrhythmias, are influenced by connections between cells via gap junctions, which allow for rapid, direct exchange of material. Using a mathematical model for coupled cells with degree-distribution variations, we explore the effects of different power-law exponent distributions on network oscillations. Our findings reveal that as the exponent (representing cell connectivity heterogeneity) increases from 1 to 3, we transition from homogeneous to heterogeneous gap junction distributions leading to the suppression of synchronized oscillations in larger networks. Our mathematical results for the synchronous solution and eigenvalues confirm that as the exponent increases, the transitive hyperedge in the network becomes more critical. Furthermore, numerical simulations in both one- and two-dimensional networks, including with and without cell size variations, replicate these findings and uncover additional mechanisms leading to the suppression of synchronized oscillations. By decoupling information about the labels and the input data, our DEGNN scheme achieves superior robustness and system performance, as demonstrated through comprehensive experiments on various classification tasks across nine datasets, showing that it outperforms recent over-the-air learning methods in terms of model robustness and predictive accuracy. Nesterov's accelerated stochastic gradient descent (SGD) has consistently outperformed its primal-dual methods counterpart when it comes to convergence. While the accelerated formulas work in tandem with fixed step-sizes selected based on prior knowledge, things become more complicated once adaptive methods like the back-tracking line search come into play. In this study, we explore the final convergence rate when the accelerated SVM loss is used with a back-tracking line search. Since classical statistical estimation problems cannot be directly categorized as monotone convex functions, a generalization to non-autonomous systems is required instead. This particularization leads to a new application of nodal reactivation for the non-autonomous version of Nesterov's accelerated SGD with a back-tracking line search, thus enabling us to prove that a specific limit is reached as $t \to \infty$, and that under certain conditions, this limit equals the ideal convergence rate for non-autonomous NAG with a step-size that varies over time. Interestingly, our research also reveals that as $t \to \infty$, the accelerated NAG with a back-tracking line search corresponds to a semi-convergent NAG with an adaptive, oscillating step-size that fluctuates over time in an alternating pattern, and reaches a limit that equals the ideal convergence rate for NAG with an adaptive, oscillating step-size, with both NAG formulations converging towards their respective ideal rates. This study finally verifies its results through an experimental validation applied to the SVM problem. In order to accelerate the convergence of SVM, Nesterov's accelerated NAG with a back-tracking line search is preferred over its NAG counterpart as well as Quasi-Block Successive Convex NAG, another method that was also explored in this study. This study's findings demonstrate the effectiveness of Nesterov's accelerated NAG with a back-tracking line search when applied to a variety of test data, and show how well its NAG formulation performs in terms of classification accuracy and convergence. Moreover, our research reveals a significant, though indirect, improvement in accuracy and convergence for the NAG formulation when compared with its Quasi-Block Successive Convex NAG counterpart, another evidence of its effectiveness. All these findings were validated using the LibSVM test data, a popular benchmark for evaluating SVM algorithms. The fundamental equations governing a bosonic oscillator in contact with heat baths are reconsidered. This formulation has far-reaching implications, as it can be used to model complex nonlinear self-oscillating systems. Furthermore, understanding the dynamics of the bosonic oscillator may also shed new light on the functionality of microorganisms capable of generating directed motion. In order to gain insight into these dynamic phenomena, it is essential to analyze the oscillator's radiation field. The paper begins by deriving an exact expression for the oscillator's radiation spectrum using the Lindbladian master equation. It is then shown that a specific measure of coherence can be utilized to determine the oscillator's radiation frequency. In cases where the coherence level is low, a simplified measure known as the emission degree is employed. By comparing the results obtained from both high- and low-coherence scenarios with existing theories, it is found that the predictions are in agreement with each other. The current research also outlines a continuous transition approach for coupling the oscillator to heat baths, thereby validating results obtained using two distinct methods for high-coherence scenarios. In addition, the effectiveness of a widely used quantum bath operator has been reassessed. The results presented here may contribute to the analysis and understanding of nonlinear self-oscillating systems and dynamical phenomena at the microorganism level. The paper includes supplementary data concerning the self-consistency of the results across various parameters. Moreover, the research offers an original method for evaluating nonlinear interaction in self-oscillating systems. The study also addresses a fundamental extension of the dynamic phenomenon known as self-localisation. This work offers a method to expedite the knowledge transfer process between a teacher and student models, involving channel pruning in a specific layer of the teacher network as the initial step. We treat this pruning task as a type of combinatorial optimization, addressing it using a cutting plane method integrated with sparsity-promoting regularization through the use of pseudo-loss. We experimentally verify our proposed approach, known as CPM-PR, on multiple teacher-student pairs and found it efficiently enhances knowledge transfer results while achieving significantly lower computational complexity compared to existing techniques. We perform further in-depth analyses of our method's outcomes, focusing on the reasons behind failed improvements in certain scenarios and identifying an interesting observation regarding the effective range of pruning rates. Furthermore, our proposed approach is uniquely situated as it does not depend on the teacher model architecture or training data. We note that our method outperforms other non-parametric baselines without reliance on these constraints, and interestingly, it tends to deliver better outcomes when the teacher model is more intricate and the pruning rate is set near 50%. We argue that this phenomenon arises from the density of the graph representing the teacher network. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the output of our method, comprising the most relevant channels and their weights, are specifically utilized for task-agnostic knowledge representation, yielding promising results when combined with existing knowledge distillation methods in two distinct settings, namely, unsupervised knowledge transfer and semi-supervised learning. Our proposed approach, including the code and data, is publicly available at https://github.com/QuantDev/CPM-PR. Past research represented these interactions through local feedback mechanisms, but neglecting longer-range relationships, even though spatial dependence is inherent. Our results indicate that incorporating non-locality leads to resilience in grazing ecosystems, reaching a critical threshold beyond which the ecosystem's response becomes dampened due to the spatial dependence. This research explores how adaptive approaches to selecting input data within dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA, influence the techniques' resistance to manipulation. We develop methods to quantify and prevent attacks on these reduced-dimensional data, particularly focusing on the effect of secretly chosen inputs. We show that conventional PCA estimators are vulnerable to attacks when the input data is tailored to the specific data set, and that this vulnerability can be overcome by using input data that is universally applicable. Drawing on concepts from information theory, we create a metric to measure a compressor's stability under varying input conditions and developed an algorithm to optimize this stability. A software Kalman filter was implemented to track the position of a magnetic token within a 2D plane, where a robotic swarm's magnetic response enables detection of changes in the token's orientation-based distance to the swarm's centroid. The kalman filter output is utilized to calculate the angular distance of each robot from the swarm's center, allowing for exploration of the underlying token localization problem. The testbed consists of 16 Arduino-powered robots, each equipped with a digital compass and an accelerometer, and their positions are accurately determined through vision-based tracking, resulting in a stable estimation of the angular distances between each robot and the swarm's center. The swarm's positional convergence to a local minimum of the potential function is observed in various simulation and experimental trials, during which the estimated angular distances are recorded and compared to their actual counterparts calculated from token position data. The mean absolute error in the estimated angular distances was found to be $3.64^\circ$ in experiments and $3.04^\circ$ in simulations. The research highlights the practical utility of a software Kalman filter within the framework of the robotic swarm testbed. Further investigation could involve modifying the potential function to incorporate prior knowledge of token position to improve estimation accuracy, and extending the research to 3D space by utilizing elevation data instead of swing-up motion. The proposed framework and associated software have been made available under the Apache-2.0 license for easy reproduction of the study's results. The project's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/sharviludwig/robotic_swarm_testbed.

For a self-supervised model to thrive on a new platform without access to new data, a well-designed, off-site pre-training is crucial. Off-site pre-training typically utilizes image classification tasks as its primary focus, but leveraging scene geometry might offer an edge in an unstructured new environment. Geometric scene understanding is an underdeveloped area, but it has the potential to provide more contextual information about the environment when compared to traditional image classification. Furthermore, reconstructing 3D scenes from a single image requires more resilient representations that can thrive in diverse new environments. Our study delves into how self-supervised pre-training based on monocular scene reconstruction enhances transfer learning for image-based navigation when the new environment lacks labels. Specifically, an off-site pre-training based on 3D reconstruction consistently outperforms those based on traditional image classification or object detection. When put to the test, our model, which is trained on 3D object reconstruction, performs better than others in image-based visual navigation with notable improvements of 2.01% and 5.21% MSE in two benchmark datasets. Our study also showcases that pre-training based on 3D object detection outperforms others in visuomotor learning, which involves teaching a mobile robot to navigate and grasp objects, and that this type of learning significantly reduces the requirement for new image data in order to achieve optimal visuomotor learning performance. Graph-explaining methods can be broadly classified into explanatory graphs and feature-based approaches. However, the former is limited by its inability to handle large graphs while the latter often produces inconsistent and redundant explanations. To address these issues, we present PGExplainer, a novel approach that explains Graph Neural Networks by interpreting their learned functions through perturbation-based analysis. This approach eliminates the scalability issues associated with explanatory graphs and eliminates the inconsistent explanations caused by redundant features. Moreover, PGExplainer provides consistent explanations by assigning labels to graph elements based on their inter-relationships and the effects of structured perturbations. Our experiments demonstrate that PGExplainer generates consistent and qualitatively superior explanations compared to feature-based approaches, and boasts improved scalability. Furthermore, PGExplainer enables a more natural explanation of adversarial examples, revealing the specific vulnerabilities that allow attackers to misclassify us. Our findings show that addressing these vulnerabilities through explanations can improve robustness. Our source code is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/blob/master/PGExplainer. State-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods excel at teaching agents to make informed decisions in complex environments, but the decisions they learn are often unclear to humans.  For instance, policies for controlling an unmanned aerial vehicle may consist of actions like "turn left" and "go faster," which don't provide much clarity to humans.  One way to increase the readability of these policies is by using symbolic reinforcement learning to teach agents discrete actions based on logical rules.  For instance, a UAV policy might be "if you're lost, go towards the nearest mountain."  We introduced an algorithm called SYROCO that analyzes the discrete actions taken by reinforcement learning agents in games like Go and Atari and uses this information to teach the agent a set of general rules that can be applied to new levels in the same game.  Our results show that SYROCO was able to discover non-obvious features that many experts missed, like "cycles in the opponent's eye movement" as a strategy for Go, and significantly improved the agents' performance using fewer rules than a competing method. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of this technique over current methods in restoring blurred images, and the code is available for review at https://github.com/davidmeredith1/image_deblurring_research/blob/main/ORBM.git. Furthermore, we also released a custom Keras-based convolutional neural network module that can efficiently replicate the results of the proposed method, also hosted at https://github.com/davidmeredith1/image_deblurring_research/blob %+/Kithub.git.

Building on existing research, we establish connections between modules with Rota-Baxter pairing and (BiHom) pre-Lie modules. This allows the direct translation of certain algebraic structures, leading to the creation of new pre-Lie modules from existing paired modules, and vice versa. Furthermore, specific types of Rota-Baxter algebras and pre-Lie algebras are related, revealing isomorphisms in certain instances. Crucially, these findings facilitate the development of graded and colored versions of pre-Lie algebras and modules, enhancing our understanding of these structures. To establish the breadth of this work, we demonstrate its applicability to integrable Hamiltonian systems, providing a unified framework for general systems through the representation theory of certain algebraic structures. As part of this, we identify specific properties and relationships of integrable systems within the context of low-dimensional systems. This work ultimately serves as the foundation for exploring additional structures, notably Hom-Lie algebras, in the context of integrable systems. Imperative programs with obscure origins frequently lack reliable specifications, yet establishing formal requirements after the fact can be impractical.  To tackle this challenge, our proposed method leverages natural language assertions compatible with predicate logic to facilitate the verification of imperative programs.  These assertions can be entered using a query interface and a structured, logical editor.  Following the introduction of program assertions, our method converts the program into a satisfiability problem, treating loop conditions as existential loops in a formula.  The satisfiability of the resulting formula is then assessed using a predicate logic satisfiability tool.  If the program satisfies the given assertions, our method employs a decision procedure to identify specific, feasible paths meeting the verification criteria.  These feasible paths correspond to models of the formula - in this context, an model represents a particular state visited by a program.  Our method utilizes the concept of explanation, at each step, to identify the most relevant states visited by a program.  Our experimental findings indicate that our method effectively meets the requirements for a non-trivial subset of programs, particularly those in context-free terms.  These findings are substantiated by our implementation of a verification engine and an accompanying interface based on client scripts and an ML-based logic engine.  Ultimately, our research demonstrates the viability of using natural language assertions for the verification of programs with imprecise origins, and the utility of our method in identifying the most relevant, program-specific information to support human developers.  Interestingly, our method also holds implications for the verification of regulated programs - in essence, our method provides an interpretation of regulatory rules consistent with predicate logic.  As such, our method serves as a model for the responsible compliance of programs with their regulatory frameworks, at the level of logical statements.  This achievement is made feasible due to the logical representation of regulatory constraints, allowing our method to identify regulatory violations and mapping the results back to the original program.  In turn, our method treats unsatisfiable formulas as program violations of the given assertions.  Consequently, our method uses the logical representation of preconditions to map the results of violation as program misalignment with its regulatory constraints, at the level of logical statements. Recent experiments investigating the properties of lipid bilayers beyond equilibrium have uncovered novel insights into the behavior of these molecular systems. Notably, findings suggest the presence of excess Gibbs layers that are larger than predicted by equilibrium data, raising questions about the accuracy of linear transport methods. This study delves into the source of this discrepancy, examining how nonlinear hydrodynamic effects, nonlinear interactions within the electrostatic layer, and finite forces on molecules influence the excess layer size. Our results demonstrate that all these factors contribute to the increased excess layer size compared to linear predictions. However, the primary effect stems from finite forces on molecules, showing that the excess layer associated with equilibrium forces is insufficient to account for the discrepancy. Conversely, finite forces generating sizes observed in experiments can only be achieved by considering finite forces in the context of nonlinear interactions. This finding has implications for the description of transport phenomena in lipid bilayers, urging the development of models that capture the critical role of finite forces in hydrodynamic and thermodynamic descriptions. This research is also available as a preprint at arXiv:2103.11955. It has been selected as a Highlights of Modern Chemistry article. Furthermore, the findings from this study have inspired discussions about the application of our finite force approach to describe molecular behavior beyond equilibrium, which is currently under review in a separate publication. This work is also related to a commentary published in Nature Chemical Biology under the title 'Beyond equilibrium: Accurate modeling of lipid bilayers required'. The authors of the study provided extensive background information on this research in a talk presented at the 201st meeting of the Division of Physical Chemistry, entitled "Beyond equilibrium: The critical role of finite forces in lipid bilayers". Accurate understanding of prediction uncertainty is crucial for reliable object detection.  Current approaches rely on calibration techniques utilizing confidence scores or prediction intervals,  but they have limited scope of applicability due to the inherent difficulty in accurately representing probability distributions within convolutional neural networks (CNNs).  The majority of object detection algorithms incorporate objectness estimation, a two-stage process that first generates proposal regions and then refines them to identify objects,  providing an opportunity to represent uncertainty in terms of both object detection and proposal regions.  In our research, we have developed a novel uncertainty estimation framework, BayesOD, for object detection by integrating Markov chain Monte Carlo methods with object detection models to sample detection outcomes based on the object detection model's distribution.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on diverse benchmark datasets have shown that BayesOD achieves high uncertainty estimation accuracy, outperforming recent methods by up to 3% in calibration measures and  1.7% in expected calibration error.  Furthermore, expected uncertainty quantiles show promising potential for use in objectness estimation,  a finding previously unreported in the literature.  The BayesOD framework is freely available at https://github.com/micmarev/bayesod.  A demo of the BayesOD method can be accessed at https://uncertainty-in-object-detection.bse-ucrio.com.  Ultimately, BayesOD provides high-quality uncertainty estimates suitable for various applications such as  object counting and instance segmentation,  and we hope it will set a new baseline for uncertainty estimation in object detection.  The BayesOD framework is freely available at https://github.com/micmarev/bayesod.  A demo of the BayesOD method can be accessed at https://uncertainty-in-object-detection.bse-ucrio.com. The transversal propagation of a wavehole through a spatial light modulator (SLM) has been investigated under an accelerating phase shift. Our research shows that wavehole transversality enables a connection between its form and how it's observed, similar to an optical fiber's behavior. To study this further, an initial analysis was conducted to identify the complete set of waveholes that maintain their shape when observed. These waveholes, characterized by specific mathematical properties, can be used to explore the relationship between spatial light and how it's detected, providing insights into the performance of SLMs, photodetectors, and other related systems. To explore this relationship, an optical system was used to investigate how waveholes change when observed. These experiments confirmed our theoretical predictions and have implications for a wide range of optical experiments. Additionally, the patterns observed in our research were found to correspond to specific features of the optical setup, further highlighting the connection between spatial light and observation. These findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of optical systems, enabling their applications to be optimized. These waveholes also offer the potential to advance the sensitivity and precision of optical measurements, opening up significant possibilities. Finally, the discovery of these waveholes raises the possibility of using them to explore fundamental limits in optical interactions, making them a valuable tool for research into these constraints. 

Key words: spatial light modulator, accelerating phase, wavehole transversality, optical fiber, inverse problem, superposition principles, optical measurements, spatial freedom, observational freedom.

Cosmic rays, primarily composed of protons and other light nuclei, collide with the Earth's atmosphere to produce a multitude of secondary particles, which in turn undergo elastic and inelastic interactions, ultimately giving rise to neutrinos and other particles. This process serves as a key source of the atmospheric neutrinos detected by neutrino observatories on the ground. The production of neutrinos can be categorized into two types: the primary process involves the conversion of mesons into neutrinos, while the secondary type involves the decay of charmed hadrons into D neutrinos. In this study, we examine the production of neutrinos and other particles resulting from the interaction of cosmic rays with the atmosphere by utilizing Monte Carlo simulations with version 2.03t of the EPOS model for cosmic ray simulations. By comparing our findings with conventional perturbative QCD and DGLAP models such as SIBYLL 2.3, we investigate the uncertainties in the atmospheric neutrino flux and their potential effect on the Icera experiment's sensitivity to the flux's high-energy end. To further explore the nuance of the neutrino production process, we generate complete phase space distributions for positron, muon, and neutrino distributions, rather than solely concentrating on the longitudinal distributions as in conventional models. Consequently, this analysis leads to an enhancement of the neutrino flux by a factor of 1.5 for the EPOS model, 1.3 for SIBYLL 2.3, and 1.1 for QGSII. Moreover, our research reveals that the uncertainty in the uncertainty of the EPOS model is somewhat reduced, with a spread of less than 20% in the neutrino flux for both EPOS and SIBYLL 2.3 models. Interestingly, our findings suggest that the D neutrino flux's high-energy end exhibits a sensitivity of ~10% to the uncertainty in the rapidity dependence of the quark and anti-quark distribution function's high momentum end. Lastly, a comparative analysis of the production of neutrinos by cosmic rays in the atmosphere using the EPOS, SIBYLL 2.3, and QGSII models has been performed. These models show that they agree with each other for neutrino production up to a certain high energy limit. However, for very high energies these models tend to diverge from each other. By incorporating a pyramidal structure into the skeleton, it facilitates swift retrieval of sensitive information from low-resolution representations, thereby enabling versatile applications for both query-based and binary attacks. Notably, the proposed skeleton yields a significant enhancement of at least $5.38\%$ in terms of DP rate compared to top-tier competitors, encompassing both weakly- and strongly-adaptive skeletons. Object-specific skeletons can be pre-trained in an unsupervised manner, resulting in a $100\%$ DP rate even at the low resolution of $12/32$, thereby showcasing their potential for demanding tasks. Mechanisms aimed at preserving data privacy utilize quantitative metrics to guarantee privacy by applying a mechanism to the data before release, preventing an attacker from determining individual data values. This research focuses on quantifying the accuracy of privacy-preserving mechanisms from which the most well-known are the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. These mechanisms release data processed by a perturbation that follows a Laplace or Gaussian distribution respectively. To offer a more comprehensive solution, this study proposes a new mechanism based on the Huber loss function that provides a more precise track record of relative accuracy and differential privacy. By using an algorithm that minimizes the Huber loss function, this mechanism bounds the relative L1-distance between before and after processing data values, thus automatically fulfilling a necessary condition for differential privacy. Furthermore, this study establishes a precise relationship between the mechanism's free variables and the achieved differential privacy. To offer a more practical solution, this research proposes an algorithm that assembles and applies a library of mechanisms optimized for various levels of desired differential privacy. Experimental results, implemented in Python using the scikit-learn library, demonstrate improved performance of the proposed mechanism compared to the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms in terms of relative accuracy for real-world datasets, while maintaining the same level of differential privacy. This research also offers theoretical and practical guarantees for the proposed mechanism's relative accuracy, based on an analysis of the mechanism's optimization problem. To offer a more in-depth understanding, this study performs an asymptotic analysis of the mechanism's performance, revealing that the proposed mechanism's relative accuracy converges to a function of the mechanism's noise level, which lies within the Pareto-frontier of accuracy versus noise variables. To offer an alternative solution, this research proposes a new mechanism called the Laplacian mechanism, which releases data processed by adding Gaussian noise scaled by the inverse of the empirical standard deviation of the data. Interestingly, this study reveals that the proposed mechanism based on the Huber loss function, the Laplacian mechanism, and the Gaussian mechanism form a hierarchy of mechanisms with decreasing relative accuracy and increasing sensitivity, which fulfills the necessary condition for differential privacy. Abstract interpretation has long been recognized as a fundamental technique in program analysis, used for guaranteeing program properties or providing accurate error messages. The zeroth level of abstract interpretation, focusing on the definition of abstract semes, lays the foundation for more advanced program analyses. The existing first-order approximation of abstract interpretation, based on polyhedra, has proven computationally expensive, leading to the development of faster approximations such as ellipsoids and sign analysis. A newly proposed approach aims to skip the complexities of polyhedra by directly implementing a more efficient ellipsoid-based approximation, yielding substantial improvements in precision over the zeroth level precision and in many cases surpassing the one-order ellipsoids approximation precision. The new ellipsoid bounds are mathematically proven to be a generalization of the zeroth level bounds and consequently as precise as them. The approach has been thoroughly tested, demonstrating high precision on a substantial collection of benchmarks. The results show that, in 73 cases out of 106, the new bounds were more precise than the zeroth level bounds and, in 52 instances, more precise than the one-order ellipsoids bounds. The tested programs exhibited no new over-approximations; all 106 instances demonstrated bounded analysis with no errors or messages and all 106 instances demonstrated accurate analysis with no errors or messages using the one-order ellipsoids bounds. The introduction of approximate ellipsoid bounds does not hinder the analysis from providing exact results as the new bounds can be switched off when the analysis is inexact, yielding results. The new bounds were implemented within the APR2 analysis tool, allowing for the verification of two previously unverifiable programs: the DC1 and the Hertz. The new bounds were also used to enable the verification of 41 previously unverifiable programs from the ZF C benchmarks. The new bounds were integrated into APR2, yielding substantial improvements for 106 programs by reducing the number of bounds checks, whereas the other 41 programs could be verified using the old bounds with a slightly reduced efficiency. The newly proposed ellipsoid bounds provide a foundation for a general ellipsoid-based approximation of abstract interpretation, opening up the possibility for further improvements in precision. The approach has been proven compatible with existing decidable complete analyses, allowing for the incorporation of more efficient approximations without compromising the analysis's decidability. The introduction of approximate ellipsoid bounds does not increase the complexity of the analysis, maintaining the same level of complexity as the zeroth level bounds. X-ray spectroscopy experiments on cuprate superconductors, performed across 25 years, have consistently demonstrated the enhancement of topological phonons following photoexcitation. Historically, these findings have been met with resistance; however, advancements in machine learning have facilitated a significant breakthrough. By incorporating these methods and comparing them to conventional machine learning approaches such as random forest, our study reveals that tetragonal perovskite phases optimize the topological phonons' energy and momentum properties. Furthermore, our research suggests that cuprate superconductors, which function without magnetic order, can be understood within a broader topological phonon framework that may also underpin the superconducting state, offering a new theoretical foundation. Additionally, our results from an x-ray spectroscopy experiment show that the phonon topological order can be leveraged to develop predictive tools for other materials, shedding light on the long-standing puzzle of high-temperature superconductivity. Ultimately, our study exemplifies the utility of machine learning in speeding up simulations within complex materials research, particularly for experiments that are too time-consuming or impossible to undertake using current technology. As the first known application of machine learning to facilitate the comparison of distinct spectroscopy techniques, our research also marks a new direction for the optimization of phase diagrams, a functional analysis of materials that holds vast potential for future advancements. A related commentary titled "Rekindling the Flame: Machine Learning in Materials Science" has been published in Materials Viewpoint (Mater. Viewpoint, 2019, 4, 133). As key elements in the study of driven quantum mechanisms, they play an essential role.  In the context of open quantum systems described by the Lindblad equation, we investigate this evolution.  We show that a particular set of coherent states remains constant under this evolution if the corresponding superoperator adheres to certain conditions.  We outline the necessary and sufficient criteria for the adherence to these conditions and provide additional examples of coherent states that maintain their stability during the open quantum dynamics, which are not related to standard photon distribution patterns.  Furthermore, we discuss certain potential applications of states with regular distribution patterns in the study of interacting elements.  We consider the scenario of two closed quantum systems, one defined by the Lindblad equation and the other by the non-Markovian master equation formulated in terms of the Lindblad equation.  We show that for non-Markovian dynamics, the condition for the stability of coherent states in the driving field is met.  In contrast, we observe that this is not the case for the Markovian dynamics.  Consequently, the condition for the stability of coherent states in the driving field does not impact the description of passive, Markovian evolution.  However, it may offer advantages in the description of non-Markovian evolution resulting from the correspondence between the non-Markovian master equation and the Lindblad equation.
