In computational modeling, especially in fields such as aerospace and automotive, consumers rely heavily on data-driven meshes to achieve precise outcomes. A mesh is comprised of basic elements, like tetrahedra in 3D, which significantly influence the result's accuracy. Since perfect meshes are rare due to inherent errors, the focus lies in minimizing these flaws. To evaluate a mesh's quality, several metrics are applied, mentioning the mesh quality measure (MQR) as an example. MQR is an abstract measure that represents a mesh's overall quality compared to a high-quality mesh. A common approach to assessing a mesh's quality involves partitioning the domain into finite elements, then computing MQR, with perfect meshes corresponding to zero MQR. However, this method requires computing many discrete values, which are difficult to compare and evaluate. To address this, the concept of weighted van Wijngaarden dodecahedron elements is proposed, allowing for the computation and optimization of MQR. By leveraging these elements and incorporating boundary conditions, the mesh can be refined, resulting in an adaptive mesh with minimized MQR. This process is currently limited by computational intensity, which can be mitigated by parallelizing the computation and incorporating a stopping criterion to prevent excessive iterations. To assess the mesh's quality in a more traditional manner, a novel measure based on a mesh-induced distance between points is introduced. This new metric is then applied to several scenarios, including a test case where the resulting meshes demonstrate improved quality, resulting in elevated convergence rates for two-dimensional and three-dimensional boundary value problems. Furthermore, the increased mesh quality has a notable positive impact in three-dimensional scenarios. As a result, the proposed algorithm offers an adaptive refinement strategy that effectively increases mesh quality in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional problems. To validate the approach, the results are compared to existing mesh refinement methods, revealing that the proposed strategy is more efficient and effective. The increased mesh quality resulting from the proposed approach leads to superior results and is less dependent on the mesh refinement parameters in three-dimensional problems, whereas it results in comparable sensitivity to these parameters as seen in two-dimensional problems. The algorithm's computational intensity can be further mitigated by parallelization on GPU platforms, yielding a high performance-speed ratio. To illustrate the performance of the proposed approach, the results are compared to current mesh refinement methods, revealing that the proposed strategy is more efficient and effective in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional problems. Even with collected data from a single trajectory, finding the optimal policy proves difficult, largely because most existing methods rely on a notion of policy similarity that prioritizes state-space accuracy. We propose that agency and visual categorizability are distinct aspects of the animacy continuum, and that they contribute independently in perceiving and understanding animacy. We utilized a conditional inference model to analyze the interactions between these components, and our findings reveal that visual categorization effectively classifies objects into animate or inanimate entities, whereas agency indicates the likelihood that an animate object is alive and capable of movement. We propose a new filtering method, referred to as the Laplace operator filter, to address inconsistencies arising from step-type simulations of PDEs, notably in polynomial-based simulations of partial differential equations. A key benefit of this proposed filter lies in its capacity to maintain the structure of the simulation, ensuring that it continues to represent solutions of a modified form of the original PDE. For example, when employing filtered step solutions of the heat equation in two dimensions, these solutions precisely match the finite difference approximations of the heat equation, up to a certain level of spatial accuracy. Moreover, we illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed filter through its application to a simulation of nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations, where significant improvements have been achieved in preserving analytically verifiable features among the filtered solutions. Furthermore, when this filter is combined with the Fourier heat filter, both components can be interpreted as forming an efficient and conservative numerical scheme, which maintains a theoretically proven, positive relationship with the step method and achieves approximately fifth-order spatial accuracy. Relevant code, including both filtered versions (in MATLAB and C), is accessible at https://git.spc.uqac.ca/JEREMIE/SPECFILTER/LATEST. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the number of possible policies increases exponentially with the number of agents, making it difficult to apply classical reinforcement learning techniques. To address this issue, some studies divide the learning process into independent stages for individual agents. However, these partitions often neglect the benefits that one stage can provide to others. In our study, we draw upon the concept of structural engineering to introduce the notion of transfer empowerment. We show that incorporating this factor enables more efficient learning in systems of multiple interacting agents. For example, when modeling the dynamics of a structural system, the model's dynamics affect the learning process of a controller, and conversely, the controller's actions enhance the learning process of the model. By exploiting these mutual benefits, the transfer empowerment principle facilitates faster convergence to optimal policies for both the model and controller. Moreover, the proposed approach leads to more reliable predictions in structural analysis, as a learned agent model helps to resist corruption from flawed observations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of transfer empowerment through numerical examples in the fields of multi-agent reinforcement learning within complex structural systems. These examples illustrate that considering the mutual benefits of transfer empowerment can outperform current state-of-the-art methods. With the increase in digital images available for training, the performance of learned models in model checking and reinforcement learning continues to improve, and the incorporation of transfer empowerment shows promising potential for future applications. The shape of an active region's magnetic field is a valuable indicator to study the evolution of the solar cycle. A specific feature, known as magnetic fill fraction, which represents the percentage of the pixel that is magnetized, is crucial in creating accurate 3D models of the magnetic field. Although modern observational data enable detailed visualization of the solar active regions, the relationship between magnetic energy density and spatial extent remains difficult to quantify. Various algorithms have been developed for 2D and 3D modeling of the magnetic field, but these have not considered the role of magnetic fill fraction, potentially leading to inaccurate global modeling. A different approach by \cite{Pietarila} directly addresses the shape of the magnetic field and its implications for modeling, which is discussed and expanded upon in this paper. We examine the significance of magnetic fill fraction in modeling and find that accounting for it leads to a significant reduction in the degrees of freedom during inverse problem modeling. Our findings show that taking the magnetic fill fraction into account yields modeling solutions that are consistent with more conventional models, such as the potential field solution, when the fill fraction is zero. Our analysis further suggests that, in the absence of magnetic fill fraction information, incorporating knowledge about the area of the modeled active region could be an alternative consideration. We also discover that, in cases with known magnetic fill fraction, the modeling solution does not converge to a single, distinct model, which is attributed to the complexity of finding a specific solution from limited observational data. Our observations, nevertheless, demonstrate that modeling active regions with known fill fraction is an improvement over not using this information at all, such as in the case of modeling the region when the fill fraction is 90%, as this leads to modeling solutions that are generally closer to each other and distinct from the PPM model. Our study thus offers a framework for exploring possible modeling solutions with consideration for fill fraction information and sheds light on existing modeling practices. As such, this research has potential to enhance 3D magnetic field modeling from vector magnetic field data, as it highlights one factor that could contribute to modeling solutions with better consistency. Although the modeling solutions obtained in this study do not converge to a specific or consistent solution, as is the case with current practices, such as in PPM and MULP1, 2, 3, our observations indicate that including fill fraction information is generally advantageous. We find that radiation from the theory impacts the stability of these black strings by altering their energy and angular momentum. We observe that the theory introduces negative effect on the energy and positive effect on the angular momentum, thereby lowering the potential energy. Consequently, this leads to softer stability constraints for charged black strings. We establish the range of stability for these strings and identify the points where the potential energy and angular momentum solidify. In this study, we investigate the reduction of complex problems involving various parameters and observations. These problems typically have an extensive computational footprint, making them infeasible to solve directly, thus highlighting the need for algorithms yielding reliable and computationally affordable approximations of the true solution. Our work encompasses two types of observations: functional and data-driven, yielding two distinct observation error concepts. Although both share a linear relationship with the noise present in the problem, the feasibility of implementing these errors depends on the specific structure of the problem and potential developments of data analysis techniques. Our research demonstrates the sequential reduction method's capacity to significantly alleviate the computational demands associated with these problems. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative upper limit for the error resulting from this reduction in the context of uncertainty quantification and the rapid propagation of ensembles. Our results encompass both UQ and propagation scenarios, providing numerical examples to elucidate the effect of varying parameter values and initial conditions on the solution as well as the influence of the observation error on these problems. Furthermore, we explore the practical implications of the results by providing upper bounds for the uncertainty quantification and propagation scenarios to shed light on the trade-off between computational affordability and solution accuracy. Our work also involves the proposed reduction method and provides numerical examples to elucidate its effect on a range of benchmark problems across UQ and propagation scenarios, showcasing its ability to drastically reduce computational complexity without compromising solution quality. Our study utilizes a comprehensive set of 11 common PDE problems, carefully designing the metric to ensure problem-specific and general results are equally represented. Our work initially focuses on functional observation error and subsequent development leverages comprehensive analysis of continuous-time Kalman filters to derive bounds for the data-driven observation error. Our research further investigates the effects of the observation error on the reduced problem and proposes the application of stochastic estimation techniques to mitigate this error. Our study concludes by exploring the potential to combine machine learning and statistical physics to develop more effective techniques for the responsible reduction of complex problems involving uncertain parameters and observations. Our work initially targets PDE-based problems but aims to broaden its scope to generic parametric PDEs and initial value problems, proposing the application of reduction methods to scenarios involving ordinary differential equations as well as the numerical propagation of stochastic differential problems. Our study provides generalizations of recent results obtained in uncertainty quantification and the propagation of stochastic differential equations scenarios using stochastic estimation techniques. Our work also explores the potential to extend recent responsible reduction developments to problems featuring uncertain parameters and functional observations, proposing the application of calibration techniques to derive accurate solution approximations in scenarios lacking initial information

Our analysis reveals that when this unphysical characteristic is removed, the previously proposed scenario is in fact impossible. Our calculation can be applied to a broad range of diffusion models, including situations where the population is divided into two types and undergoing either subcritical or supercritical diffusion. Understanding semantic relationships is a crucial aspect that has long been studied in natural language processing, with a recent surge in interest due to its extensive applications in natural language understanding and sound event recognition. This research tackles the challenge of predicting semantic relationships between sound events and their attributes using a novel approach based on graph-based learning. The proposed method utilizes a multimodal transformer network that leverages features from both sound events and attributes to forecast semantic relationships, with the additional benefit of incorporating an attention mechanism to determine the important features to focus on. To further improve the model's performance, we analyzed different sound event and attribute attention patterns and found that using class-specific attention yields better results than using class-wise or localized attention. The proposed approach demonstrates superior outcomes on the DOA dataset, with a high F1 score of 0.903 (5% improvement over the current state-of-the-art), accompanied by robust sound event and attribute attention patterns. Moreover, we observed that the attention mechanism is directed more towards the sound event than the attribute, as expected, with the added insight that it favors the direction towards the source of the sound, showing its effectiveness in predicting the desired dialogue of sound event attributes. Therefore, this research demonstrates the efficacy of graph-based learning with a multimodal transformer network in accurately forecasting semantic relationships between sound events and their attributes. The analysis of the generated sound event attribute attention maps also underscores the importance of understanding semantic relationships in the context of language modeling. This paper introduces an isolation forest (iForest) implementation in Python and evaluates its effectiveness in generating highly anomalous data for the challenge. The iForest algorithm works by recursively dividing the input data into distinct subsets, attributing anomaly scores based on leave-one-out methods. In experiments, the authors discovered that boosting isolated anomalies enhanced data anomaly amplification, revealing iForest's robustness across diverse input data and its capacity to facilitate effective anomaly amplification when compared to a random anomaly model. The enhanced iForest algorithm achieved top performance in the challenge with test scores of 0.9302 (validation) and 0.9206 (test). The proposed technique, along with accompanying code and data, are available for further research. The implemented algorithm consists of iterating through the training dataset once, with computational complexity influenced by the number and depth of decision trees. Through several trials, the anomaly detection performance of the enhanced iForest algorithm was demonstrated to be stable and robust across different hyperparameter settings. In comparison to other algorithms, the performance of the enhanced iForest algorithm surpassed those applied to the validation and test sets, including LightGBM, DarkRank, and DarkMultiSVM. Furthermore, the enhanced iForest algorithm showed promising results when applied to two medical datasets, retracing the steps of in vitro screening for compound-based prion therapies and in vivo compound-based prion therapies to treat bovine spongiform encephalopathy. In a final set of experiments, the anomaly scores generated by the enhanced iForest algorithm were utilized to evaluate the efficacy of the top two ranked methods in the challenge: DarkForest and DarkMultiSVM, by treating them as proximity functions to determine their ability to position distant data points far from isolated anomalies. The results showed that the anomaly scores generated by DarkForest and DarkMultiSVM placed regions of interest in relation to isolated anomalies, however the enhanced iForest algorithm successfully amplified anomalies in the data such that the test scores of DarkForest and DarkMultiSVM increased from 0.8463 and 0.8322 to 0.9002 and 0.9043 respectively. Consequently the enhanced iForest algorithm successfully delivered anomaly amplified data that improved the performance of these algorithms, highlighting the potential utility of the enhanced iForest algorithm in medical imaging and other domains. The computational time of the enhanced iForest algorithm was found to be 0.085 seconds for the dataset used in the challenge, allowing it to scale effectively for general-purpose anomaly amplification in most domains. Image search and duplicate detection face significant challenges due to rapid
growth in data volume and varying image styles. Existing solutions suffer from
low precision and scalability. This research introduces active indexing to boost the
robustness of image copy detection, using a pre-trained neural network to
generate distinctive multi-style images that improve identification accuracy.
Active indexing enhances detection precision by at least 3.3 times and scales
efficiency 7.6 times better than current methods. Furthermore, it increases the
overall detection speed up to 40 times due to reduced computation required for
each query. Active indexing also supports searching images that have been
modified stylistically, while preserving the original data for applications
involving self-supervised learning. Our work includes a demo site that allows
users to upload images and identify similar ones (style and content). The code
for active indexing is available online at https://github.com/josh-vo/image-indexing. 

Keywords: image search, duplicate detection, indexing, deep neural network,
content search, style transfer.

An electron in a strong magnetic field experiences significant motion when interacting with vacuum photons, causing it to recoil. Research has shown that this effect is linked to both the electron's kinetic angular momentum and the growth of its wave packet in phase space. We propose that this phenomenon be identified by the parameter $\tau_*$, which represents the time it takes for this growth to occur. We have discovered that $\tau_*$ is consistently in proportion to the magnetic field strength when applied to various electron models, including the Dirac and Weyl equations, as well as the relativistic electron's spin-dependent and spin-independent kinetic energies. Our findings align with both the initial stage of this phenomenon, in which the electron moves in sync with its initial orientation, and the intermediate phase, in which this alignment gradually decreases. We have developed a general method to calculate the localized density of the electron's kinetic angular momentum and the corresponding $\tau_*$ parameters for any given model based on its polynomial dependence on the magnetic field strength. Our studies demonstrate the usefulness of $\tau_*$ in analyzing both the vacuum photon-recoil effect and the growth of the electron's recoil from the vacuum photons in phase space. Further investigation of this phenomenon through $\tau_*$ may uncover new insights into this phenomenon. As an extension of this investigation, we have discovered that the electron's recoil may lead to the observation of a nonlinear change in the electron's susceptibility to an external electric field when the electric field strength is sufficiently strong and the electron is in a state of non-localization. This phenomenon, which results in the electron's reduced linear susceptibility compared to the vacuum condition, could potentially be detected through optical studies on hole-doped 2D semiconductors. A comparable effect may also occur in the heavy-hole exciton in a quantum well under a strong magnetic field, where the linear susceptibility is diminished due to the hole's anisotropic recoil when the external electric field is applied. Our analysis reveals that the heavy-hole exciton may serve as an efficient tool for studying the vacuum photon-recoil effect and the growth of the recoil from the vacuum photons in the context of this phenomenon. Our work offers an innovative approach to the phenomenon of electron localization caused by interaction with a strong magnetic field in 2D semiconductors and hole-doped 2D semiconductors. Our studies also serve as a foundation for future research on the phase transition from a metallic to insulating phase in the context of this phenomenon. Experiments conducted on small-scale games produced high accuracy rates for N-FPN models, which also exhibited greater robustness in the face of corrupted input data when compared to a baseline approach relying on a general neural network model. Further analysis revealed that N-FPN models' parameter distributions displayed inherent properties of a normal distribution, and fine-tuning these parameters enabled the exploration of broader neural distribution spaces, enhancing model resilience. Building upon this discovery, NFPS were successfully extended to larger-scale games, and our findings suggest a meaningful correlation between the structure of the loss landscape and the primary axis of the parameter distribution. This newly characterized distribution is referred to as the principal axis of variation. This research marks the first instance where the axis of variation in a loss landscape has been explicitly characterized and named. Interestingly, our findings for both the prediction of game equilibria and the classification of game types suggest that higher confidence levels associate with narrower distribution spreads. The source code for the NFPS is made available at https://github.com/micboly/NashFixedPointNetworks. Our data and model specifications are hosted on https://figshare.com/ - a data sharing platform. Additionally, our model's performance on specific game types can be accessed through https://pub.dev/ - a Python code repository, for efficient reuse and further investigation. Lastly, our research contributes a comprehensive dataset of 18,000 games referred to as GEM. This dataset is currently publicly accessible through https://github.com/GEM-dataset - a GitHub repository. Our research paper detailing the results is currently under review and will be updated with a link to the accepted version upon publication. Our research contributions include advancements in two key areas: predicting the confidence levels of game equilibria and classifying game types. Additionally, our research lays the groundwork for future investigations into NFPS through comprehensive analysis of the GEM dataset. Our research utilizes this dataset to uncover novel insights into neural networks that adopt a fixed point root-finding technique, providing an alternative to standard gradient-based optimization methods. Our findings reveal that these networks not only accurately predict game equilibria and classify game types but also exhibit inherent properties of a normal distribution in their parameters, which can be leveraged for enhanced robustness. By extending fixed point networks to larger-scale games, our research reveals a meaningful correlation between the structure of the loss landscape and the primary axis of variation, contributing significant knowledge to the field. This study focuses on how applying dimensionality reduction techniques impacts the intersection of statistical learning and causal inference, particularly for high-dimensional datasets. We demonstrated that well-known dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA, CORAL, and SCC, inherently make a strategic trade-off between introducing bias and boosting estimation power. We developed two methods for measuring the correlation between original and reduced-feature covariates, as well as the optimal sample size required for reliable inference in dimension-reduced causal effect estimators. Our results revealed that popular high-dimensional causal effect estimators, such as twang and hdmed, reach their optimal performance when using features obtained from CORAL. Additionally, we established that the maximum likelihood estimator is an efficient and robust estimator for categorical outcomes, offering higher correlation, better bias, and greater estimation power compared to twang and hdmed. We verified these findings through simulations and a real-world cancer patient example, which measured the effectiveness of surgery and radiation therapy combinations. Our analysis found that the maximum likelihood estimator yielded the most accurate results in this application. This work highlights the potential for further exploration at the intersection of statistical learning and causal inference, providing a framework for determining when to prioritize reducing bias or increasing estimation power in causal analysis. Our code and data are publicly available on our GitHub repository. As the primary advantage of this research lies in its conceptual framework, it has the potential for extension to a broader range of estimators, such as propensity score matching and instrumental variable methods. Furthermore, our dimensionality reduction techniques can be adapted to experimental datasets, offering further opportunities for improvement. Our primary contributions at the data level are the introduction of two metrics for measuring the optimal sample size required for reliable inference in dimension-reduced causal effect estimators, and the demonstration of the preferable characteristics of the maximum likelihood estimator for categorical outcomes. While our findings may seem intuitive to experts in the field, they provide a foundation for the causal inference community to adopt a more systematic approach to choosing between bias reduction and increased estimation power. Our primary contributions at the methodological level are the development of new metrics for measuring the optimal sample size required for reliable inference in dimension-reduced causal effect estimators, and the extension of a previous theorem to accommodate a broader class of estimators. Our work can be extended to propensity score matching and instrumental variable methods, providing a valuable framework for the propagation of uncertainty in these applications. Our research offers a novel application of dimensionality reduction techniques to causal analysis and learning, enabling the propagation of uncertainty in causal effect estimates for categorical outcomes. This work presents an innovative method for detecting stealthy attacks on Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems by leveraging real-time observations to create a set of potential systems. Adversarial attacks aim to deceive these models by implementing subtle changes to the system's gain matrix. Our proposed approach monitors the distance between predicted and actual system outputs in real-time, effectively constraining the potential system models within a bounded area. This methodology facilitates continuous online monitoring, allowing the detection of stealthy attacks in real-time and with improved accuracy compared to existing methods. Simulation results demonstrating the efficacy of this approach are provided. Additionally, the potential application of this method to detect attacks on Linear Time-Varying (LTV) systems is explored. Automated document summarization has become increasingly critical as the size of available text continues to grow, with the goal of condensing lengthy, unstructured documents into compact, summary-length passages.  Despite significant advancements in state-of-the-art models like BERT, pre-existing document summarization models suffer from one primary drawback: they fail to learn from their own mistakes during the summarization process.  To address this limitation and optimize document summarization, a novel approach called GAE-ISumm is proposed, which integrates a pre-trained BERT model with a type of BERT-based pre-training task called the GAE.  The GAE-ISumm model is then used to create summary passages by leveraging its optimized representation of words within the context of the original document.  Experimental evaluations of the proposed model, based on the popular CNN/DailyMail dataset, demonstrate that it outperforms three distinct benchmarks for summarization: standard ROUGE metrics, a more sophisticated metric called BLEU+LF, and a metric that assesses fluency in the summary passage.  Furthermore, a comparative analysis of various combinations of the proposed model components reveals that the combination of the GAE-ISumm model and the pre-trained BERT model outperforms individual extraction-based and generation-based document summarization models.  Finally, the proposed model is observed to robustly function in the presence of noisy summaries, which may have significant implications for document summarization in a variety of real-world applications.  Overall, the performance enhancement of the proposed model suggests that its integration with other document summarization models could lead to the development of more accurate summarization tools.  Future directions for the proposed model include the exploration of its generalizability to diverse text types and domains.  Future research should also prioritize the evaluation of document summarization models in controlled environments to isolate sources of noise and test the model's robustness in such scenarios.  Future research may also invest in the development of other GAE-based tasks beyond document summarization to fully capture the pre-training benefits afforded by this type of task. This research applies an ensemble modeling approach to improve the resilience of neural networks in the presence of uncertain labeling. By utilizing high-performance GPU capabilities, a Monte Carlo simulation is carried out to generate multiple iterations of labeled data for training, which in turn facilitates the calculation of confidence thresholds for robust training. The proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on well-established datasets, revealing a substantial boost in overall classification precision and the reduction of false positive and false negative rates. Notably, the accuracy of the model is further solidified by the increased use of positive instances, evident from the increased TPR and FP rates. Moreover, the efficacy of the model is exemplified through two real-world biomedical applications involving Alzheimer's disease detection and drug resistance prediction in tuberculosis, showcasing its potential for significant real-world impact. The associated code is freely available online.

For semiflows with expanding properties, both uniformly and non-uniformly, research demonstrates that certain transfer operators fall short in exhibiting exponential decay of correlations. However, in cases where the expanding dynamics are based on a finite number of equations, it has been discovered that the transfer operators' kernels do exhibit exponential decay in the context of total variation within a transition interval of limited scope. Despite the limited applicability of this finding, it serves as a significant stepping stone in establishing key hypotheses related to the Mackey inequality, ultimately leading to the proof of an essential condition for the existence of Gibbs measures in finite-dimensional, non-uniformly expanding systems governed by non-autonomous dynamics. These results have been generalized to encompass deterministic and non-compact systems as well, thereby offering valuable contributions in the former case. In a related context, researchers have investigated the properties of $L^2$-invariance for certain classes of Gibbs measures in non-uniformly expanding systems. Interestingly, it has been discovered that the transfer operators' kernels play a crucial role in establishing an important bound involving the squared $L^2$-distance between consecutive iterates of arbitrary test functions. Consequently, this finding helps establish the $L^2$-invariance of Gibbs measures in non-uniformly expanding systems with compact spatial domains. Moreover, using a novel approach based on $L^2$-random walks and taking advantage of the underlying transfer operators' kernels' ability to map $L^2$-functions as bounded operators, researchers have successfully devised an explicit recursion formula enabling direct construction of Gibbs measures in non-uniformly expanding systems. These contributions have been generalized to address additional classes of systems including those subject to random and non-automous dynamics, as discussed in the accompanying paper by B. Barrau, C. Colinet, and D. Jarusek. Specifically, this work explores the establishment of Gibbs measures in non-uniformly expanding systems displaying hyperbolic and quasistable properties, facilitating its application in addressing critical open questions related to the former case. In their paper, the co-authors utilize functional laws of large numbers and limiting properties of the empirical measure to establish the convergence of the Gibbs measure to the full measure of maximal entropy for non-uniformly expanding systems. This work has been generalized to encompass the space of observed processes and is discussed in further detail in the accompanying paper. A subsequent discussion with E. Turchin regarding his work on generalized transfer operators for non-autonomous systems is also presented in the appendix

A computational analysis of SU(6) quantum spin systems featuring 20 sites, situated on triangular and kagome lattices, has been carried out using the density matrix renormalization group method. The study examines various energy and spin structure factors, which are influenced by different spin configurations in these systems. By comparing the results for triangular and kagome lattices, the impact of symmetry between near and far interactions on the properties of these systems has been determined. The findings also suggest the presence of spin liquids in these many-spin systems, characterized by uniform structure factors across all energy levels for both triangular and kagome configurations. Moreover, the study explores the emergence of spin liquids in smaller systems and their potential connection to SU(2) quantum spin systems, which feature different scaling of energy and spin gaps. The investigation of spin liquids in smaller systems has also revealed the onset of spin gap at a system size of 36 for triangular and a wide range of system sizes for kagome, as well as the presence of plateau structures in the energy spectrum that grow logarithmically with system size for triangular and a linear relationship for kagome. Finally, the study examines the emergence of spin liquids in larger systems and the presence of spin gap in a wide range of triangular and kagome configurations, regardless of the number of sites. The findings suggest a transition from paramagnetic to spin liquid phase in both triangular and kagome, accompanied by the presence of spin gap and a standard energy gap for triangular and a wide range of gapped states in both triangular and kagome configurations. The research discovered two distinct spin liquids in both triangular and kagome, distinguished by their energy and spin structure factors, which can be categorized as spin-Liquid I and spin-Liquid II. The study found that spin-Liquid I is characterized by its uniform structure factors and energy spectrum across an extended region of energy levels for both triangular and kagome, whereas spin-Liquid II emerges in an range of energy levels above the spin gap for both triangular and kagome, distinguished by its distinct energy spectrum. The study discovered that spin-Liquid II's energy spectrum features a pattern consistent with spin wave excitations for both triangular and kagome, as well as a linear relationship for kagome. The research found that spin-Liquid II emerges in an range of energy levels below the spin gap for triangular, characterized by its distinct energy spectrum, which can be divided into two distinct regions separated by a gap consistent with spin wave excitations. In recent years, researchers have employed various statistical techniques to calculate sample-sized requirements for inferring an average treatment effect while maintaining a controlled false discovery rate (FDR). Existing methods typically apply a uniform FDR constraint to multiple group comparisons but fail to consider the effect of multiple testing when calculating sample sizes. This paper presents two novel statistical techniques that take the intercorrelation of data sets into account to calculate optimal sample sizes for identifying an average treatment effect with controlled FDR in the context of multiple group comparisons. The proposed methods utilize two distinct types of dependence models, namely the generalised correlation framework and the stochastic block model, that can be used to evaluate various levels of intercorrelation among data sets. The techniques involve generating a hierarchical probability distribution from the family of null bihomogeneous distributions and employing the Tied-Null-Hypergeometric distribution to calculate the probability of success for multiple group comparisons. Building upon this foundation, the authors derive the distribution of the sum of correlated binomial variables and utilise it to determine the requisite sample sizes for achieving an FDR-controlled alpha-level under correlated data sets. The methods presented in this work cater to experiments involving any number of data sets and consider varying levels of intercorrelation among them. The methodology's efficacy is demonstrated through numerous examples and simulations, which further highlight its utility in calculating sample-sized requirements for different correlation levels among data sets. The methodology's key advantages and differences over existing methods are highlighted in the commentary. The algorithms and statistical techniques discussed in this work are implemented in the publicly available R package StatInf, which includes the necessary functions to calculate sample-sized requirements for an average treatment effect with controlled FDR in the presence of intercorrelated data sets. The package's functions can be utilized through the command SnR_package("infCOR") followed by the required parameters for calculating optimal sample sizes for identifying an average treatment effect with controlled FDR in the presence of intercorrelated data sets. The statistical techniques presented in this work have further applications in facilitating data sharing by utilising the calculated probability of success for multiple group comparisons to identify replicable results with controlled FDR in the presence of intercorrelated data sets. The public domain release of the R package StatInf facilitates data sharing of the statistical techniques discussed in this work. The statistical techniques presented in this research can be extended to calculate sample-sized requirements for detecting other effect sizes by generating probability distributions from the family of null bihomogeneous distributions. In the field of natural language processing, determining the authenticity of natural language data is becoming an essential skill with numerous practical applications. This research proposes an evaluation framework to assess the authenticity of conversations by assessing the level of neural entrainment between utterances within a conversation. The proposed framework leverages pre-trained Transformer models to generate embeddings that represent individual sentences and passages, which can then be analyzed using various metrics to quantify the degree of entrainment. Experiments conducted on both human and machine-generated conversations, including those produced by GPT2 and GPT3, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in distinguishing authentic from fabricated conversations using entrainment-based metrics. Furthermore, analysis of the findings reveals that the underlying linguistic structure of authentic conversations is characterized by relatively low yet increasing lexical entrainment, whereas fake conversations exhibit inconsistent and abnormally high lexical entrainment levels. Building on this insight, the research proposes an innovative metric called Neural Entrainment Distance (NED) to measure the authenticity of conversations. By fine-tuning the pre-trained Transformer models on human-generated data using NED, the experiments reveal the potential for significant improvements in the accuracy of machine-generated conversations, suggesting numerous potential applications of this metric in evaluating and refining automated text and conversation generation systems. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/JasonJackKarlson/Neural-Entrainment-Distance. This study marks a significant advancement towards developing more realistic and natural-sounding text and conversation data by leveraging advanced natural language processing techniques to validate and refine generated data. In doing so, the research provides valuable insights into the linguistic and structural characteristics of authentic and fake conversations, ultimately contributing to the crucial skill of natural language authentication in the field of natural language processing. The findings of this research suggest that the degree of neural entrainment can be leveraged as a valuable metric in evaluating not only conversation, but also text generation more broadly, across machine and human-generated data. By shedding light on the unexplored domain of natural language entrainment, the research opens up new avenues for exploring the intricate world of human language, ultimately enabling more sophisticated and sophisticated human-computer interactions. The research provides valuable practical implications for evaluating and refining data and models in the fields of automated and computer-based applications, highlighting the need for more realistic and natural-sounding conversation and text that can be met by leveraging recent advancements in natural language processing techniques. Visual understanding of human actions is a crucial aspect of reading body postures in videos. Existing action recognition systems' performance has been significantly enhanced through the incorporation of fine-grained action details. However, existing action segmentation pipelines are largely dependent on supervised datasets, limiting their widespread use. A new cooperative network is proposed to parse actions in untagged videos, using an innovative co-occurrence-based approach to identify action sequences. Experimental results on existing datasets reveal that the proposed cooperative network outperforms current action segmentation benchmarks. To address the existing shortage of labeled data, the study proposes a self-supervised learning strategy for a co-occurrence-based network, increasing the network's performance by up to 14.7% action segmentation accuracy. A novel dataset, DSHP, containing dense action sequences and corresponding human postures across various action categories is introduced for enhanced action understanding. DSHP dataset, containing 5000 videos with dense action sequences, is combined with existing action datasets, increasing existing dataset instances by 12 times. The study's resources, including the proposed cooperative network, DSHP dataset, and training code, are available at: \url{https://github.com/ying1613/Cooperative-Net}. A visualization tool for the proposed cooperative network is provided at: \url{https://www.kalculating.com/cooperative-net}. The study's findings indicate certain action sequences can serve as a reliable and clear explanation of how different actions unfold. It is hoped that this research will contribute to the advancement of easier and more transparent human action analysis in the future. This paper addresses the issue of adapting a model to a domain without any reference data, a challenge that poses significant problems for practical applications. As existing methods require reference data to learn target domain properties, they fail when this information is unavailable. We address this problem by developing a domain adaptation approach for unsupervised source data scenarios. We employ two self-supervised learning techniques: contrastive learning and exoplanet prediction, to extract source domain features that are resistant to target domain adaptations. Moreover, we incorporate self-supervised target domain prediction along with contrastive learning to exploit target domain correlations. The proposed approach outperforms existing methods on three benchmark datasets, including glycine recognition, Saint Bernard image classification, and cancer recurrence prediction. Moreover, the research shows that the selected technique has the potential to solve other unsupervised adaptation challenges. It is established that the absence of source data poses difficulties for traditional unsupervised adaptation methods that heavily rely on image to vector conversions. Therefore, the research suggests a new understanding of unsupervised domain adaptation: a challenge requiring learning a vector to image conversion. The research findings indicate that the problem can be easily resolved if one converts the source data into image format and incorporates visual components from the target data. However, the adaptation challenge persists if the conversion process involves significant losses. It is observed that the application of unsupervised domain adaptation with self-supervised learning techniques is not a panacea for all domain adaptation scenarios. Interestingly, the research shows that the selected technique has the potential to solve most of the unsupervised adaptation challenges. Hence, the research suggests exploring more advanced self-supervised learning methods to develop effective domain adaptation strategies. The gas core reactor is a nuclear reactor concept based on an enclosed fusion reaction in a small, pressurized container. Efficient operation depends on maintaining high pressure to minimize thermal loss, typically in the range of 100 to 150 atmospheres. Our challenge is in simulating the gas core reactor since it involves the intricate interplay of large-scale atomic reactions, electron collisions, and energy transfer within a high-pressure environment. We have addressed this complex problem using two distinct Monte Carlo techniques that integrate atomic and ionic processes into existing particle-transport codes. These code enhancements include detailed models for ionization, recombination, and energy exchange that utilize local thermodynamic equilibrium assumptions whenever possible. Our simulations, conducted at various pressures, highlight the significance of non-equilibrium ionization and recharge for accurate predictions, which varies significantly with pressure. Additionally, we found that precision in particle transport becomes a critical factor at high pressures due to increased sensitivity. Our findings align with experimental data available at lower pressures, which suggests that the main governing reaction at equilibrium is the Breit-Wigner Fritsch resonance, while at non-equilibrium conditions, resonance width is broader than in equilibrium. Furthermore, we examined x-ray spectra both with and without non-equilibrium conditions to determine the impact on thermodynamic characterization. Our analysis revealed that the gas core's plasma state can be safely considered in thermodynamic equilibrium below 120 atmospheres, but above this pressure, non-equilibrium conditions start to dominate, which may lead to reduced energy output. Our simulation models are publicly accessible through the GAMERS code repository on GitHub, located at https://github.com/GAMERS-EU. Similarly, the Monte Carlo techniques described are also applicable to other high-pressure plasma environments beyond the gas core reactor. They may be of interest in studying other nuclear reactor concepts, such as high-pressure MHD reactors, accelerated ion beam targets for fusion, and other high-pressure plasma experiments. Our work showcases the Monte Carlo techniques' robustness and versatility in addressing problems in plasma physics research. In the future, these techniques will be extended to simulate the gas core's non-local energy exchange to optimize its operation. Our investigation into the reason behind the observed energy loss in the gas core, which is typically at 10%, may also be able to shed more light on this specific efficiency gap. The efficient operation of the gas core relies on reducing this energy loss, addressing it may further promote the gas core as an attractive nuclear energy source. Logic programs can include aggregates, which are analyzed using a three-step process: interpretation, modeling, and modeling checking. Answer Set Programming employs the modeling phase to generate solutions for aggregates. However, Answer Set solvers do not handle aggregates as part of their core logic and require special handling. Our focus is on developing grounding algorithms for logic programs that include recursive aggregates, which involves creating specialized tree data structures for each solver and determining the most efficient distribution of logic programs' clauses. Our work demonstrates that using trees for aggregates can be combined with existing preprocessing techniques to generate models for programs that include recursive aggregates. Our findings indicate that using trees for aggregates is generally an effective approach, but we also identify scenarios where it may not be necessary, allowing us to generate models using nominal logic representation instead. Our algorithms are part of the ASP-ID solver, which incorporates symbolic debugging features, and our study also examines modeling checking using tree data structures for aggregates. Our work demonstrates that using trees for aggregates can yield symbolic state representations that facilitate modeling checking. Our experiments involve comparing the efficiency of using trees for aggregates against other approaches, including nominal logic representation and grounding without aggregates, which involves modeling checking for programs with aggregates using Horn programs as an alternative. Our findings show that using trees for aggregates can be an efficient approach, especially for programs that use aggregates extensively. Our study also demonstrates the feasibility of using tree data structures for aggregates that involve recursive functions, which may have an overall positive impact. Our work concludes by outlining future research directions, which include exploring other approaches for grounding aggregates, implementing debugging features for recursive aggregates, and integrating our work with other Answer Set solvers. Our aim is to contribute theoretical and practical aspects regarding the grounding of logic programs that include aggregates, as well as their application and deployment within the field of Reasoning about artificial intelligence. Our study also showcases the importance of aggregates within the domain of artificial intelligence and reveals areas where research is still in its infancy, thus highlighting opportunities for future exploration. It is demonstrated that when certain conditions are met, these expectations serve as upper limits to mutual information. The second method converts the polynomial equations into corresponding generator networks that can be trained using sample data to make mutual information estimations. In higher-order topological insulators, the connection between the band gap in the bulk and gaps at the edges follows a mobile first-order phase transition. We investigated the impact of disorder on this phenomenon, focusing on how it alters the phase transition type and disordered mobility gaps in 3D and 2D topological insulators. Disordering key parameters such as hopping amplitudes or nearest-neighbor weights with a uniform distribution led to a shift in the phase transition type to a second-order one, accompanied by a potential change in mobility type. Notably, we discovered that disorder consistently increases the size of mobility gaps in both 3D and 2D topological insulators, and this enhancement occurs regardless of whether the phase transition remains a first-order one. This increased size of mobility gaps in bulk and edge systems can be attributed to a spread in localized states' energy distributions triggered by disorder. The observed phenomena were verified through numerical simulations and analysis of the inverse participation ratio. The presented study offers insights into understanding disorder's effect on properties of higher-order topological insulators. Further research could involve exploring other types of disorder, such as randomly localized states' origins, and its potential to induce a bulk topological phase transition. Additionally, investigating the impact of disorder on thermoelectric properties, particularly in 3D and 2D HTIs, could reveal intriguing connections between disorder, transport phenomena, and mobility-like effects at finite temperatures. Moreover, the ability to tune and manipulate edge states' energy and spin densities could lead to applications in spintronics and topological quantum computing. The observed phenomenon of cross-over in bulk and edge mobilities may also indicate a universal behavior common to other types of topological materials. A possible extension of this work involves investigating how these principles apply to other types of topological insulators, such as 2D and 3D TI models. The study also offers a framework for understanding disorder's effect on topological states in quantum systems. As one section becomes increasingly large, two key indicators of entanglement - the logarithmic negativity and the entanglement of mutual information - initially rise steadily. Ultimately, they converge towards a critical threshold, which is roughly equal to the amount of photons present in one of the sections. As a subsystem approaches the same large size as the total number of photons, entanglement essentially disappears. This phenomenon can be understood through the analysis of a particular universal subspace within the system and its characteristics in each half. Specifically, the entangling capability of this subspace is limited to a certain "bonding" capacity, which determines the maximum achievable negativity. Notably, when the subsystem reaches a size comparable to the total number of photons, the entanglement reaches its maximum value. Furthermore, another universal subspace that encompasses the entire system and is available through projector sampling reveals that system entanglement is primarily driven by individual excitations' interactions rather than their collective behavior. Notably, a positive amount of entanglement can be maintained due to limitations in projector sampling, even when the excitations are non-interdependent. This subspace also provides insights into how entanglement behaves under unitary transformations, ultimately failing to observe any significant effects from universal coupling. The study's findings have been supported by several numerical experiments. To further explore entanglement properties, an open-source quantum circuit simulator was used to create and apply unitary gates based on varying coupling strengths. As a result, no noticeable entanglement fluctuations were observed when the coupling strength deviated from the ideal case. The presence of inherent limitations in realistic quantum circuit implementations poses an essential challenge in understanding quantum properties and their uniqueness. The study's findings also shed light on optimal strategies to maximize entanglement using quantum circuit simulators, which can be leveraged to improve these quantum processors. Specifically, a method was discovered to maximize entanglement by maximizing the mutual information between parts of a system and implement an optimal unitary circuit to achieve this maximization. Notably, a quantum processor's unique structure, characterized by its unequal qubit sizes, can be utilized to enhance entanglement between parts of a system and corresponding photons. The study's implementation details and associated code are documented at the supplied repository. The study's findings have been made available in the study's note section. The research presented in this dissertation contributes meaningfully to the understanding and development of quantum properties in photonic systems.

This HBSNN has a unique architecture in which the hidden states of the network concurrently track the system's true state and the beliefs of state variables optimized for optimal control, while its outputs forecast the system's observations. This approach is based on the principle of using the system's beliefs as part of the loss function. By back-propagating the loss, the HBSNN updates its hidden states in such a way that they align with the optimal control beliefs and the system's true state. This method has been tested and demonstrated to achieve state of the art results on a well-established benchmark for controlled Hidden Markov Models (HMMS) and has also been successfully deployed in the field of robotics by enabling a robot to effectively plan and execute trajectories based on partially observable environmental conditions. Enhancing the amount of contributed data might require concessions on individuals' privacy, as this involves adjusting the compression method used in the aggregation phase. Conversely, the relationship between data quantity and learning efficiency in the lossy data generation process under DP remains unclear, and resolving this could offer new avenues for optimising algorithm performance given limited data. The use of machine learning in enhancing table extraction from documents has become a crucial step in leveraging information. Traditionally, tables in documents have been distinguished by their visual attributes, with deep learning techniques further developing this approach. Nevertheless, to extract tables comprised of unstructured text, a different method must be employed. In this context, we present TABNET, an innovative solution that combines graph neural networks and attention-based learning for table extraction. By analyzing the structural relationships between words in a document, TABNETWORK identifies tables comprised of sequential information, thereby enabling the selection of relevant data based on semantic considerations. Through an analysis of the HTRF-ESTabL2 dataset, we demonstrate that TABNETWORK outperforms existing techniques, achieving a 3.5% improvement in F1 score for blind table recognition and 4.1% for blind table localization. These static filters utilize machine-learning methods, such as a support vector machine, trained on prior dynamic classifications. This approach provides several benefits, including the elimination of need for a direct connection to dynamic classification modules, reduced memory and computational speed requirements, and the ability to be implemented using binary hardware. We have developed a method for creating an optimal filter, given a specific false positive rate, by finding the shortest possible hyperrectangle in the input space that excludes negative examples. Our proposed algorithm allows for efficient computation of an optimal filter and can be applied to continuous input data. We have also presented an approximation algorithm for cases where computational resources are limited. Experimental results show that the filters produced by our methods significantly outperform traditional bounding-based filters in terms of accuracy and efficiency, both in terms of memory and speed. We have tested our methods using a dataset from the field of visual quality control, where we achieve an average true positive rate of 95% at a false positive rate of 0.1%. This has significant real-world applications, including a 7-fold improvement in speed over traditional bounding-based filters. This approach can be applied to various dynamic classification techniques, including deep neural networks. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed filter on deep neural networks, we have found that an implementation on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays yields a 2.6-fold improvement in speed over a 64-bit central processing unit, while using the same amount of hardware resources. To address voids with extremely high density ratios, two modified approaches have been implemented: a dynamic relaxation method for coarse resolutions and a quasi-static recovery method for finer resolutions. The former uses wind to push voids away from roots, while the latter uses upwind weighting and dynamic Taitian equations to approximate phase compressibility. This study aims to address these limitations by exploring unsupervised convolutional neural network models for classifying patient sub-groupt and measuring Alzheimer's disease progression. Initially, four unsupervised loss functions - contrastive loss, contrastive loss with metric learning, multi-signal fuzzy entropy, and fuzzy entropy - were tested over a period of time to assess their respective ability to reduce data dimension and facilitate learning from label-free data. Recent findings have uncovered significant long-term dependencies in randomly shuffling finite datasets, contradicting existing theories such as the Flamingo Hypothesis. To tackle this issue, we present the Backward Dropping Algorithm, a novel, theoretically grounded method for creating artificially dependent datasets from independent data. Isometric embedding is often used to represent complex data in a simplified manner, and recently, it has been applied to the medical imaging field to create easily interpretable results from black-box models. Nevertheless, the fact that not all data points can be mapped to a 2D or 3D Euclidean space in an informative way presents an issue for evaluation. Consequently, we suggest utilizing conformal prediction to provide predictive intervals for the output of black-box models used for segmentation. By representing uncertainty in the segmentation result as an uncertainty region instead of a point, we can circumvent the problem of non-injective mappings. Our approach enables the meaningful evaluation of these models, which is crucial for clinical decision-making and guiding treatment decisions. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using an example that involves calculating the volumetric radius of tumors. In this case, we find that the most informed predictions from three-dimensional U-Net models agree with those from pixel-level supervision about 58% of the time, whereas they agree about 73% of the time when the input data undergoes downscaling. Moreover, the volume of the segmented rods recovered using our proposed method is on average 0.81 cubic units, which indicates moderate accuracy. The data and code for this analysis are publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/graciewang26/conformal-prediction-for-quantitative-metrics. The continued growth in data reservoirs relating to DNA hybridization experiments highlights the need for an updated approach to analyzing them more effectively than current static-based methods. In our previous work, we introduced the RBB-NA algorithm for nucleic acid research, which uses a reinforcement learning agent to train on experimental data and refine its accuracy. Building upon this foundation, we further enhance RBB-NA through several key updates. Firstly, we optimize its neural network components to boost its capacity for complex nucleic acid structures. Secondly, we enhance the efficiency of RBB-NA's training process by dividing it into two stages to improve its overall outcomes. In addition, we automate the process of optimizing RBB-NA's hyperparameters using the HyperOpt library to make its training more streamlined. Furthermore, we develop a specialized evaluation metric to assess perfect matches and mismatches in nucleic acid structures, thus facilitating RBB-NA's direct comparison with alternative techniques. In our experimental analysis, we demonstrate the practical applications of our updated approach in three distinct scenarios, which involve simulated, non-coding RNA, and DNA sequence data. In the simulated setting, our results reveal that RBB-NA produces a high level of agreement with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods in terms of nucleic acid structure prediction. In the non-coding RNA scenario, our results show that RBB-NA yields structure predictions that closely align with X-ray crystallography at a lower cost, thus exhibiting its potential as a fast and efficient alternative to Monte Carlo methods. In the DNA sequence case, our results indicate that RBB-NA's fine-tuned parameters lead to structure predictions that are closer to experimental results than Monte Carlo methods, which underscores its versatility in enhancing DNA sequence prediction accuracy. In conclusion, our updates to RBB-NA offer a versatile tool for nucleic acid structure prediction that can be adapted across different nucleic acid types, which is beneficial for research into DNA hybridization and non-coding RNA phenomena. The updated RBB-NA code is publicly available at https://github.com/harsh19tr/RBB-NA-Upgraded. Chromatic aberration, a distortion inherent in lenses that separates and scatters light, has historically been difficult to simulate in digital cameras. In the field of computer vision, this distortion is often overlooked due to its diminutive size, however, we contend that its subtle manifestation yields notable compositional benefits. Compositing with chromatic aberration can enrich visual narratives by distinguishing warm and cool events, thus requiring artists to consider incorporating it seamlessly into their work. When interpreting real-world images, we employ a novel approach that accurately estimates chromatic aberration by leveraging pre-existing depth maps, resulting in the first feasible implementation on regular consumer-depth cameras. In support of our assertion that chromatic aberration is a valuable visual effect, we provide a range of examples demonstrating its effectiveness in a variety of applications. Furthermore, we provide an efficient and optimized Python solution for chromatic aberration simulation, offering it under an open-source license. The associated code and dataset can be found at the following repository link: https://github.com/guim.alejandro/CA_sim. Additionally, a sample tutorial is available at https://docs.alejandro-gui.github.com/CA_sim.

We expand upon this concept to series composed of functions and obtain convergence under $C^\alpha$ norms by imposing restrictive assumptions on those functions. We also demonstrate the generation of such series can facilitate the calculation of particular infinite sums or integrals, as seen in problems involving pseudodifferential operators and their connection to generalized Airy functions. A specific example illustrates an infinite series in terms of $C^{\alpha \text{ } (1+)}$ with $\alpha>0$, which yields the generalized Airy integral series. We further utilize these series in the context of pseudodifferential operators with distributional symbols and show even moderately dense grids can lead to exact representation of their associated functions, even with only a seemingly random selection of terms. We also establish a connection between $C^\alpha$ classes and the space of strongly convergent series, where the latter's properties align with those of Chebychev polynomials and algebraic series. A special case sees the convergence of $\alpha$-harmonic series for $\alpha>0$, where visualizations of exceptional sets with exceptional density were obtained, possessing Preprint: http://www.mat.ufrgs.br/torre/exceptional_set_refutation.pdf. This paper explores the theoretical implications of a soft $Z_2$ symmetry in the $Z_n$ extended Standard Model for the Higgs boson's n-fold mixing, particularly focusing on n=2. Through a two-loop analysis, we examine the effects of this mixing on the kinetic term of the Standard Model gauge bosons and derive the related constraints based on the electroweak precision observables. Additionally, we bracket the possible mass differences between the primary and secondary Higgs bosons, and we investigate the decay of the lighter Higgs boson into two photons, also considering its visibility in associated production with a Standard Model fermion pair. This analysis reveals that a soft $Z_2$ symmetry does not introduce significant electroweak precision issues but can produce the 125 GeV Higgs boson decaying into photons, with its visibility ranging from 3 sigma to 5 sigma, depending on the mass of the lighter Higgs boson. Lastly, the mass of the lighter Higgs boson is bracketed up to a few GeV, and its coupling to a Standard Model fermion is found to be mildly violated compared to the standard model prediction, with these deviations increasing with the mass of the lighter Higgs boson; however, these effects become minimal as the mass of the lighter Higgs boson exceeds 15 GeV. These findings imply that a soft $Z_2$ symmetry in the $Z_n$ extended Standard Model offers a viable explanation for the Higgs boson's decay into photons while maintaining consistency with electroweak precision observables concerning the kinetic term of the Standard Model gauge bosons. Furthermore, the mass of the lighter Higgs boson is bracketed, and its coupling to a Standard Model fermion is found to be at best ten percent larger than the standard model prediction, with these effects becoming even less pronounced as the mass of the lighter Higgs boson increases. Lastly, the associated production of a Higgs boson and a Standard Model fermion pair can serve as a probe for constraining the mass of the primary Higgs boson, with this analysis yielding an upper limit of 30 GeV, corresponding to a 5 sigma confidence level. This finding implies that a soft $Z_2$ symmetry in the $Z_n$ extended Standard Model is a viable yet conservative model that can be distinguished from the standard model's parameters by dedicated experiments involving associated production at 13 and 14 TeV collider energies. We explore the concept of universal solutions within the context of data exchange, allowing for the possible absence of solutions for certain input databases, even with adapted versions of the cover property. Our investigation focuses on two specific aspects: the existence and consistency of universal solutions for keys that comply with certain conditions, including the coverage property and a subset called 'B-covering'. Additionally, we examine three distinct scenarios: a scenario where a key complies with the coverage property, one where a key's parts satisfy the coverage property, and a subset called the 'B-scenario'. Our key findings include the existence of universal solutions for the 'B-scenario' and the presence of consistency in this same subset. Moreover, we demonstrate that checking the consistency of universal solutions for a particular key is an NP-complete problem when that key complies with the coverage property, but this complexity issue is reduced to co-NP if that key's parts satisfy the coverage property. Our study ultimately concludes by discussing the potential expansion of the concept of universal solutions to diverse entity relationship schemas. Our results suggest that consistency is achievable in certain instances when applying the coverage property to a particular relationship scheme. Moreover, we observe a disparity in the existence of universal solutions for entity relationship schemes versus other data exchange settings, as well as an instance where the complexity of checking the consistency of universal solutions reaches an exponential complexity when the entity relationship scheme complies with a specific condition. Our study presents an overview of previously published results in this field, thereby offering novel insights and contributing to previously unexplored questions regarding the consistency of universal solutions for entity relationship schemes. Our final point concerns the possible presence of 'inconsistent' universal solutions for specific data exchange settings, along with an illustration of an entity relationship scheme that exhibits this inconsistency, thereby confirming an earlier hypothesis posited by Lei Zhu and Divesh Agrawal in their paper published in 2013. Our investigation further sheds light on the distinct properties of data exchange settings by showing that two particular cases, one being the entity relationship scheme and the other being the coverage property, differ via an entity relationship scheme that complies with the coverage property but exhibits the absence of a consistent universal solution, thereby demonstrating the existence of 'inconsistent' universal solutions for this subset. Our study concludes by presenting two problems open to investigation, with Problem 1 focusing on determining whether the consistency of universal solutions is generally achievable for the 'B-covering' class, with Problem 2 concerning the same issue but for the scenario when that key's parts satisfy the coverage property. FPIO is based on the VGG16 architecture and incorporates a fully convolutional per pixel per label conditioner. To enhance its per position representation, FPIO employs a piecewise implicit conditioner incorporating iterative self-attention. In our study, FPIO was trained using only 500 annotated samples from SberBank Data, and it significantly outperformed previous few-shot parsing models. After cross-validation, the best FPIO model was applied to the task of answering compositional questions after parsing, where it delivered consistent results comparable to those of its training objectives. Consequently, FPIO achieved better overall performance in combining parsing and answering tasks compared to individual per position IAs. To our knowledge, FPIO represents the first per pixel per label few-shot parsing model. Our extensive analysis involved evaluating FPIO on four datasets: SberBank, LDPAR, Pattern-based Parsing, and the WikiGame. The code used to implement FPIO is available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/keylul/FPIO. Our study confirmed that FPIO's per position per label conditioner facilitated enhanced compositional parsing abilities. Our research further demonstrated that FPIO's per position per label conditioner is adaptable to existing parsing tasks and can be used to improve task-specific per position per label models. Research has highlighted the benefits of diverse training data for speech recognition. Nevertheless, measuring data diversity and its impact on model robustness remains a complex challenge. In this study, we investigate ways to quantify diversity in speech recognition datasets and assess its effect on model robustness. We extend this analysis by exploring the relationship between diversity and model performance across various aspects, including speaker variation, topic shifts, and out-of-domain speech. We present simple metrics to quantify data diversity based on speech features and transcripts and conduct an experimental investigation on a large Google speech recognition dataset. Our results show that increasing diversity in training data enhances model robustness, and effective metrics accurately capture this relationship. We observe that data variability concerning speech features correlates better with model robustness than variability in transcripts. Furthermore, our study indicates that the bulk of hidden state variations in internal model representations are driven by relatively few tokens. Taken together, our findings provide insights into the role of diversity in enhancing speech recognition models and guide the development of tailored evaluation metrics to assess model robustness. They also inform efforts to fine-tune models for out-of-domain applications. Importantly, our research bridges the gap between recent advancements in analyzing neural networks' internal workings with the goal of improving whole-system performance. As a final contribution, our study provides practical guidance to data providers and trainers on leveraging diverse training data to improve speech recognition models. It suggests that data enrichment strategies, including augmentation and combining datasets, can be effective in achieving this goal. Importantly, our analysis reveals that data enrichment may also reduce the complexity of the model's parameter space, facilitating efficient adaptation to out-of-domain speech. We conclude that the bulk of hidden state variations in the model are driven by relatively few tokens.
